item.title: The Met Has Put the Oldest Existing Copy of the Odyssey on Display - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Likely prompted by the runaway success of a certain classically oriented movie in theaters this summer, the Metropolitan Museum of Art has returned the oldest preserved fragment of The Odyssey to one of its galleries, where it can be seen and appreciated after a long time out of view. The relic is now on display in Gallery 162 in the museum’s section devoted to Greek and Roman Art.

In a round-up of Odyssey-related collection treasures on its website, the Met describes the relic as the first early Ptolemaic fragment of the text ever discovered and notes: “Dating from around 285–250 BCE and made in Egypt, this fragment is beautifully inscribed using a combination of charcoal and water via a stylus on papyrus—one of the most popular materials for writing in antiquity—and contains three lines that do not exist in today’s standard text.”

In a new video on the Met’s Instagram page, Sean Hemmingway, the curator in charge of the Met’s Department of Greek and Roman Art, attributes those three lines to oral recitations by disparate bards who were known to “occasionally embellish and have different versions of these stories.” He also shows how the papyrus fragment is viewable in frontal and back views.

Comparing the story to the legacy of Odysseus himself, the Met’s round-up reads: “Like the Greek warrior, this object reminds us that the telling of The Odyssey itself has taken its own distinct journey through history.”

item.title: Colombia’s Museo de Arte de Pereira Closes due to Extensive Earthquake Damage - ARTnews.com
item.description:
As workers race against the 72-hour, so-called golden window to rescue survivors from collapsed buildings following Monday’s devastating 7.4 earthquake in northern Colombia, the region’s museums are also in serious jeopardy.

On Monday evening, Alejandro Garces, a curator at the Museo de Arte de Pereira, posted photos on Instagram of the damage sustained to the museum that is located about 220 miles west of Bogotá and is the principal art institution for the states of Caldas, Risaralda, and Quindío, which together form the “Zona Cafeteria” or the country’s coffee triangle.

The images show whole walls collapsed, leaving its interior with sweeping views of the city. Jagged X-shaped fissures ripped through galleries, exposing bricks and concrete and leaving paintings and framed prints clinging to teetering walls. An exterior wall of a building adjacent to the museum’s 177-person theater fell on the roof causing it to cave in and leaving a gaping opening. Twisted lighting tracks and dangling electric cables pierce the blue summer sky. 

In his post, Garces wrote, “70% of the cultural infrastructure of Risaralda is in ruins.”

Pereira, the largest city of the Risaralda Department with a population of approximately 500,000, is located just 35 miles from the epicenter of Monday’s earthquake. Registering a magnitude similar to the one in Venezuela this past June, Colombia was fortunate that much of the force was blunted by the 64-mile depth of the epicenter causing the seismic energy to weaken as it traveled to the surface. The Venezuela quake, by comparison, had a depth of about 12 miles.  

The cities of Pereira and Manizales, located about 30 miles northeast, are among the most severely affected by the disaster and so far account for more than half of the current death toll. As rescue workers search for the missing and families grieve their departed, survivors are also grappling with the loss of homes, businesses, and sites that comprise cultural life.

“In the area affected by the earthquake, they have identified 14 museums that have been affected,” Libardo Díaz, director of the Museo Rayo in nearby Roldanillo, told ARTnews in a phone interview. Díaz’s institution has also experienced significant damage. “Of these, the one in very grave condition is the Museo de Arte de Pereira.”

The Museo de Arte de Pereira is the largest contemporary art museum in the region. Initially founded in 1974 as the Center for Contemporary Art, it became a museum in 1996 after the passage of “la ley de la cultura” which established a fund for the promotion of art and culture. With those funds, the organization was able to expand and rebrand as a museum, opening a new building designed by Colombian architect Willy Drews Arango.

The museum’s 520-piece collection includes works from late 20th-century Colombian artists like Oscar Muñoz, Olga de Amaral, Beatriz González, who passed away this past January. The museum is “not only significant for Pereira—it’s quite significant for the much larger region,” said María Paz Gaviria Muñoz, who was director of Bogotá’s ArtBo fair from 2012 to 2024 and is from Pereira. “It’s been key to the decentralization of arts in the country, beyond Bogotá, Medellín, and Cali.”

Engineers’ inspection of the Museo de Arte de Pereira on August 11 determined that the damage from the quake was extensive “but not structural,” according to Rosa Ángel, a board member who is in charge of the institution’s emergency response. Even though the beams and columns of the museum are sound, many walls and roofs will have to be rebuilt, demanding a “reconstruction that is going to be very complex,” she said. 

Given the extensive damage, the museum is closed to the public. How long the museum will remain closed, how much reconstruction will cost, and how the museum will pay for it is still unknown.

Though technically operating as an independent nonprofit, the museum is largely sustained with government funding from the city, state, and the Colombian Ministry of Culture. The damage from the quake comes as “reductions in already very limited national and [local] government funding have left the museum in a complex economic situation,” Gaviria Muñoz said. “So now, as we start talking about the need for reconstruction [we must also consider that] it will need very substantial funds to continue operating.”

The far-right Espriella government is only days into its tenure. Elected based on an agenda to cut government spending by 40 percent, it’s unclear how—or even if—the Ministry of Culture will step in to support the Museo de Arte de Pereira, Museo Rayo, or any of the other 12 damaged museums. ARTnews has contacted the ministry for comment.

The scale and abruptness of natural disasters like Monday’s earthquake make for stark contrasts and difficult choices. “The city is trying to rescue people from the rubble. People are homeless, without things—it’s very, very difficult,” Ángel said, “but we also have to fight for our cultural infrastructure and do the work to protect it.”

But as the Zona Cafetera rebuilds, advocating for the museum to reopen is important, she said, because “culture is the cement that keeps us united as a society.”

item.title: Roman Artifacts on View at Syria’s Damascus Citadel Following Repatriation from France - ARTnews.com
item.description:
When French President Emmanuel Macron visited Damascus in early July, he pledged to support the country’s rebuilding efforts in the wake of former President Basher al-Assad’s overthrow 18 months prior. While the main focus of the visit was economic—Macron discussed reviving Syria’s banking sector and returning more than $50 million that had been confiscated from the Assad family—the diplomatic gesture also involved the return of 23 artifacts that had been held in France since their initial loan for an exhibition at the Arab World Institute in Paris 15 years ago.

According to a report in the Associated Press last month, Macron himself transported the artifacts on the presidential plane and delivered them to Syria’s National Museum. The objects date from the ninth millennium BCE to the 14th and 15th centuries A.D., and were originally loaned from museums in Damascus, Aleppo, Latakia, and Palmyra.

Now, a selection of these objects are on view as part of a summer festival at the Damascus Citadel, a former military fortress and UNESCO World Heritage site that recently reopened.

According to Turkiye Today, the objects are on view in the citadel’s Throne Hall and include funerary sculptures, relief objects, and other ancient Roman artifacts.

Abdurrahman Amer, a festival official, noted the significance of the exhibition. “People are visiting this citadel for the first time in their lives. At the same time, the return of these historical artifacts and their reunion with Syrians after many years is creating great happiness and excitement.”

item.title: Italian Police Recover $10 M. Worth of Artworks by Cezanne, Matisse, and Renoir - ARTnews.com
item.description:
If 2025 was the year of the museum robbery, perhaps 2026 will be the year of the recovery. On Friday, Italian police announced that they had recovered three artworks stolen in March from the Fondazione Magnani Rocca near Parma in Northern Italy, according to Reuters.

The recovered paintings are Paul Cezanne’s Still Life with Cherries (1890), Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s late-career Les Poissons (1917), and Henri Matisse’s Odalisque on the Terrace (1922).

Their collective value is said to be in excess of $10.4 million. A report by the BBC in March noted that Les Poissons, the sole oil on canvas, is worth the most, valued at around €6 million ($6.9 million). The Cézanne and Matisse are both works on paper.

The Cultural Heritage Protection Unit of the Carabinieri, the national gendarmerie of Italy, found the works in an apartment in Parma; nine Moldovan nationals have since been placed under investigation.

The painting were stolen on the night of March 22 into the morning of March 23. Police released a video of the robbery, which appeared to show a three-minute robbery in which two thieves entered through a window and grabbed the works off the wall.

Also known as the “Villa of Masterpieces,” the Fondazione Magnani Rocca houses the collection of Italian critic Luigi Magnani. Magnani established the foundation in 1977, before his death in 1984, and named it after his parents. His collection includes works by Titian, Dürer, Rubens, Goya, Canova, and de Chirico.

item.title: Kit Fitzgerald, Pioneering Video Artist With a Painter’s Sensibility, Has Died at 73 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Kit Fitzgerald, a visionary video artist with a sense for the music and motion of painting, died on August 3 at 73. The news was announced by her husband and longtime creative partner, Peter Gordon, on Instagram. He wrote that she “fought a rare and aggressive cancer, but always maintained a sense of beauty and wonderment.”

A trained painter, Fitzgerald imbued electronic art with the unruly touch of brush and canvas—vivid color, dynamic light, stuttered gesture—resulting in what she termed “technology with a humanness.” Her paintings were populated by people and places reduced to wild lines and strange confines; interposed with sound, they provided spectral stages for the preeminent composers, poets, and choreographers of the last three decades. Beginning in 1984, she and Gordon brought their production design to Tokyo, where they performed with Ryuichi Sakamoto; to the Sydney Festival, for an Arthur Russell tribute directed by Gordon; and to La Mama in New York City, for a landmark live show with Max Roach.

“She was one of ten kids in a family that enjoyed each other’s company,” Gordon told ARTnews of her childhood in Springfield, Massachusetts. “She was never one to sit alone; I think that’s why she liked collaboration and performance—it involved working with people.”

In 2020, Fitzgerald created projections for The Mother of Us All, a collaboration between the Juilliard School, the New York Philharmonic, and MetLiveArts: “video quilts that played joyfully with the Engelhard Court architecture at the Met,” as the show’s director, Louisa Proske, shared online.

Fitzgerald was at the vanguard of American artists critically engaging with television as a medium; she and John Sanborn were among the first artists to receive commissions from PBS and the BBC. Their celebrated collaboration, Interpolation (1979), spliced everyday sounds and images into cacophonous clips, as if broadcast from network news in another dimension—”exaggerated and intensified with unsettling skill,” according to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, which acquired the one-channel video in 2023.

Her body of video work resisted easy explanation. “What is it about? There’s no puzzle, there’s no trick, it’s about itself,” she told MTV in 1982, ultimately describing the experience as an abstract symphony. As the New Yorker once wrote, “Her images are avant-garde painting of a high order.”

Twenty years into the video movement, institutions had begun to take notice. “Video Art: A History” opened at the Museum of Modern Art in 1983, curated by Barbara London and featuring more than 250 artists, among them Fitzgerald. MoMA followed the seminal survey with “The Arts for Television” in 1989, the first of its kind to examine television as a site of creative deconstruction. Sixty-seven artists presented videotapes—encompassing literature, dance, music, theater, and more—as alternative programming; Fitzgerald contributed To Sorrow (1984) to the music section, alongside Laurie Anderson, Robert Longo, and Julie Hayward.

Inspired by the writing of Thomas Hardy, with a score by Gordon, To Sorrow was a meditation on humanity’s self-isolation from nature. Its clips of the lush but lonely Irish pastoral landscape were sourced from another video performance, The Return of the Native, and conveyed some of her cinematic signature: a tracking shot or slow focus from an unexpected vantage point, like a car window; a meticulous pan of shifting light at the far horizon. At one point in To Sorrow, horses amble towards the camera in a slow-motion sign of life.

“Kit was a wonderful artist and a joyous person,” Barbara London wrote online, sharing her condolences.

Her work, Gordon reflected, “doesn’t superimpose artifact on top of the real thing. It’s like having a conversation and you listen to what they have to say—some people just talk over the conversation. Kit would listen.”

Fitzgerald’s work was exhibited at the Whitney Museum of American Art, including twice in its biennial, and broadcast at institutions far beyond, including Moderna Museet, Stockholm; Gallery Watari, Tokyo; the Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston; and the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam. A Smith College graduate, she taught at Concordia College, where she created and led the New Media Communications and Digital Production undergraduate and graduate programs. Her work was distributed by New York’s Electronic Arts Intermix.

She is survived by her husband and their son, Max.

item.title: Shirley Tse and Dana Berman Duff's Breathing Moons - Hyperallergic
item.description:
When sculptor Shirley Tse was invited by her former student Anna Hrund Másdóttir to produce an original exhibition at her cooperative gallery King and Bang in Reykjavik, her first thought was to invite her friend and former teacher, the film and video maker Dana Berman Duff, to collaborate with her. 

Geography, landscape, desire and time are some of the interests these two artists shared. The result is an extraordinary manifestation of physical elements — breath, moon and tides — that bind us and the universe. 

Working under the name “Relational,” Tse and Berman Duff's exhibition The Universe Breathes Us was first staged at Kling and Bang in 2025, and again this summer at Shoshana Wayne Gallery in Los Angeles. Both iterations included a live choral performance of an original song by Berman Duff and her husband, the composer-musician Alan Duff Berman. Seeing it for the first time, I was struck by the deceptive simplicity of each of the elements and the subtly seamless ways that they animate each other. In Tse’s photograph “Orkney Moon” (2025), a soccer ball covered in rice paper rests in a green summer field on a Scottish island. Reborn as a moon, it migrates into a series of sculptures that fill the main gallery, contained by projections of Duff’s videos on opposite walls. In “The Other Side of the Moon Is Not Dark” (2025), a giant moon slowly rotates, and in “The Breathing Ocean (Portal)” (2026), the moon meets a video of the original Icelandic choir fracturing into a kind of northern lights. 

In an adjacent room, film and sculptural elements combine in the surprisingly moving installation Sun and Moon (2025). Suspended by thread from the gallery ceiling, Tse’s rice-paper moon casts changing shadows in the white light of Duff’s 16mm projector. The tail end of a big reel of film flaps incessantly.

I’ve followed and written about both Tse’s and Duff’s work for more than two decades. The Universe Breathes Us felt like a new and exciting departure. On August 4, we met at the gallery to talk about it. This conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity.  

Chris Kraus: It's such a beautiful show and there's a lot of different things to talk about, but first, the title Relational — you joined up to form a collective?

Dana Berman Duff: Yes, we did.

CK: But it’s not a traditional collaboration — instead, you made your work in dialogue with each other’s. It’s a really interesting thing that happens maybe unconsciously when artists and writers work in proximity. How did the show come about?

Shirley Tse: If you watch the eight-minute Orkney Moon video in the hallway, you’ll get the context of our collaboration. I started researching tidal turbine power during a residency in Scotland two years ago. I’m really into sustainability in my recent practice and tidal power is a form of renewable energy. Initially, I thought this new work would be all about engineering — you know, the turbine blade, etcetera. But then I came across this sentence that completely changed my direction: “Tidal power is the only form of power we harness from the Moon.” Tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon, together with the Earth and the Sun: in other words, relational force. In that moment, I remembered reading in the book Yoga Anatomy a quote that talks about breathing: The most basic fact of breathing is not my body sucking air into my lungs and releasing it. Rather, when I inhale, the weight of the atmosphere pushes air into my body. And that immediately breaks the subject-object relationship! I was invited to do a show in Reykjavik, and I didn't want to do a solo show. I wanted to make this show a relational force with another artist that I admire so deeply. So I invited Dana to collaborate with me. 

DBD: I just wanted to mention that it wasn't a conventional collaboration — we each made our own pieces. It's a relational collaboration. My pieces wouldn't exist but for Shirley’s. 

CK: Sorry to be technical, but just to clarify things here, what is a tidal turbine? 

ST: Just like a wind turbine that turns blades to create energy for electricity, a tidal turbine is a form of renewable energy. You put a turbine through tidal currents, and the force of the tides pushes the turbine to generate energy. 

CK: That's amazing. 

ST: Yeah! Instead of solar power or wind power, it's lunar power! I thought that was so poetic and I had to make art about it. 

DBD: Hence all these moons.

CK: The exhibition notebook contains a lot of emails you both wrote while you were conceiving the show. I was really struck by something you said, Dana, in an email to Shirley about how one reason you left sculpture behind was that you wanted to work with time as an element, and you could only do that in film and video. 

DBD: Yes, but I started working with time long before moving to film. I was very influenced by both Buddhism and structuralist film. I realized that I was frustrated with making objects that were supposed to last forever. So I wanted to work with impermanence, though I didn't think of it that way then, but I started making sculpture out of liquids and things that would fall apart or degrade — and all of these works no longer exist. Film was the medium where I could really use representation and control time and explore the experience of looking — that it's very much like meditation. It's like being present in the moment for what's happening, yeah, like breathing.

CK: There's this insane calculation in the notebook where you’re dividing the rotational speed of the moon by its — volume? 

DBD: [Laughs] Essentially, it's just a scale exercise. I took the size of the real moon, the diameter of the real moon, scaled it to the size of that projected moon on the wall, and I ended up with a certain ratio. Then I took 29.5 days, which is the time it takes for the moon to fully rotate, and multiplied that by the ratio to arrive at two hours and 40 minutes.

CK: So it's kind of a math poem.

DBD: It is totally structuralist. For me, every choice needs to be based on some kind of structure, not on taste. And so I had to find a rational structure for this projection. And I was delighted that it turned out to be two hours and 40 minutes, which means that you can barely see it moving. It’s very like my other 16mm films. Barely moving. 

CK: You could say that breath is the overall theme of the show. Would you agree?

ST: Yes. Breath. Breathing.

CK: Everything’s held in place by the breath and that quote from Yoga Anatomy that you put on the wall, that “breath enters us all by itself” — we just have to allow it. How did you think about this while you were building the show?  

ST: Relational force, manifested by breath, is at the center of this exhibition. When you see a body moving, it's easy to think that that movement comes from the body itself, but the movement actually comes from the relational differences, the differential, between two bodies. So there's no A or B. It’s the dynamic that produces the illusion of A and B. This is very poetic, but I think it’s actually a critical stance as well. Our world is in a very chaotic moment right now. I believe that it is the individualist, isolationist mentality that got us into this mess in the first place. Our model of the relational, no-self, runs counter to the idea of the individual that's isolated, separate, and always wants to assert power over other things. 

CK: Yes, but I’m still curious how the Bobbing Moon sculptures that fill the main room came to be. The soccer ball moon from Orkney Moon has migrated onto suspended mesh squares that form rectangular fields. How did you arrive at these constructions? 

ST: The sphere form comes from the Orkney Moon project. The photograph of the white ball on the grass in Scotland, the hanging paper sculpture in the Sun and Moon installation, and the video on the small monitor all share the same title, Orkney Moon. Because I wanted to show that this sphere is not just an object; it’s an event, in different forms. 

Dana’s moon projection shows the moon from the sun’s, not the Earth’s, perspective. From there, you see the moon in 360 degrees, without any dark side. I thought seeing the moon from this perspective was so beautiful that I responded with the “Bobbing Moon” sculptures. Even though they don’t physically move, they suggest movement, resting in a delicate balance between their weight, tilting angles, and anchoring stones. My sculptures have always been fragile because I want them to reflect the fragility of our life-world. 

During the opening, people knocked the sculptures off their balance. People were kind enough to help me reset the sculptures by holding onto them. However, I had to gently ask them, "Let go, let go!" Without letting go, you will never find your center. 

DBD: Yes, and in this exhibition, we completely suspend “individual authorship”: All of the works are produced by Relational, even though many of them weren't even touched by the other person's hand. But because Shirley's mind exists, my work exists here. It’s all completely the product of the interaction. 

ST: Material and shape choices I used in the sculptures adhere to my current practice of not buying any more new materials. So all of this material was already in my studio, leftover from past projects. The tent poles make the sculptures collapsible- more sustainable in terms of transport and storage.

CK: Shirley, I think the use of sound in this exhibition is something new — but Dana, as a film and video maker, sound has always been an important element. How did you conceive the pervasive sound in this exhibition as a force?

DBD: Sound is a way I can work with time. I think of sound as another image space. When you hear something, you see something in your mind. As you walk through this installation, you hear breathing, and that would influence your body in this space. 

CK: It's like being inside a giant body. 

DBD: But then there's also, really at Shirley's urging, gradually coming in is the sound of waves, of the ocean, so we can bring it back to the tidal idea, and then there's a weird grinding noise of the underwater energy collection turbines. It's not a pretty sound, but I thought it was ethical to include it. And then there's a little musical piece composed by Alan that I wanted to add because it's soothing and calming. And then it returns to the choir. 

CK: Okay, the last question is, the sculpture in the other room is just so incredible. I just stood in the middle of it and it was so completely immersive and engaging and brilliant. The flapping of the 16-millimeter film, the football, the shadow that it cast. It's like every idea in the notebook and the exhibition is contained in those simple objects. I mean, that's a real coup. So can you talk about how you arrived at that?

DBD: I thought I should make the sun for Shirley's moon.

Since I work in 16-millimeter film and I have these projectors and I wanted to invoke something that's kind of apocalyptic and sad, that is, the disturbing sound of a 16-millimeter projector running out of film. Flap, flap, flap. And to most of us the sound is alarming and that's the feeling I wanted to invoke: “Oh no! The film is over!”

ST: When I came up with Orkney Moon the “sculpture,” I thought it was the most beautiful thing I ever made, because I did not make it myself. I began without any plans, letting go of my ego and my prejudice. I observed what the children were doing and folded their interests into mine. And then Orkney Moon made itself! It was a solid three-dimensional thing in the beginning, but when I took the rice paper off of the football for my niece Sandra to "conserve" it, it became a drawing. When it was kicked by my nephew Tiger, it picked up chlorophyll and the soil. It was a drawing, not by me, but a drawing by the soil, the grass, and the action of kicking. I don't want this “thing” to be just sitting there as an object in an exhibition, so it needs to be activated, as an event. My dear friend Jessica Bronson suggested making a book that tells the story or gives it context somehow and that inspired the idea of making the exhibition notebook. Perhaps this project exists both in physical space and literary space that gives people the feeling of containing the whole world.

item.title: New Digital Archive Honors Gaza Journalists Killed by Israel - Hyperallergic
item.description:
“Anas was one of the journalists who ran into the line of fire,” reads a translated eulogy by independent journalist Doaa Shaheen about her late colleague, prominent Al Jazeera reporter Anas al-Sharif, 28, who was killed alongside four other journalists on August 10, 2025, by a targeted Israeli strike on their media tent near al-Shifa Hospital.

“He covered events as they unfolded because he believed the Palestinian narrative was worth this effort and exhaustion,” Shaheen's voice note continued. “Our stories are worth all this suffering. They deserve our presence on the front lines, documenting the truth.”

Shaheen's oral eulogy is one of several devoted to al-Sharif on a new digital memorial for Gaza's martyred journalists. Developed and launched by the Writers Against the War on Gaza (WAWOG) yesterday, August 12, “The Living Record” is an oral archive for remembering and recognizing the small but extraordinarily endangered community of Palestinian reporters, especially as the number of Gaza press fatalities by Israel since October 2023 hovers at around 240.

The Living Record launched with individual memorial pages for 24 slain journalists. Profiles and eulogies for another 21 journalists will be added throughout the fall, and the archive will continue to grow in acknowledgment of the historically high yield of targeted press fatalities during the Gaza genocide.

item.title: Top Executive and Senior Sales Director Leave Pace Following Gallery’s ‘Restructuring’ - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The shakeup at Pace Gallery isn’t over. Just two months after the gallery laid off roughly 50 employees in a sweeping restructuring, two of the executives who helped shape Pace during its years of rapid expansion are headed for the exit.

Amelia Redgrift, the gallery’s chief communications officer, and Dani Forest Brandi, a senior sales director, have both resigned. Where they’re going remains under wraps. Sources told ARTnews, however, that both have already landed senior roles elsewhere in the art and culture world.

Forest offered one clue, saying that her new position will be formally announced in September. “My time at Pace was invaluable,” she told ARTnews. “I joined Pace and had many wonderful years working closely with the Glimchers, their inspirational artists, and innovative team. I look forward to the next chapter of our relationship and bringing that wisdom to my new role.”

Their departures add another chapter to what’s becoming one of the biggest resets in the gallery’s history. In June, CEO Marc Glimcher dramatically shrank the business, cutting staff across departments and reducing Pace’s artist roster as part of what he described as a necessary correction after years of expansion. Neither Redgrift nor Forest was part of those layoffs.

In many ways, the pair arrived together. Redgrift was recruited from Hauser & Wirth in late 2019, just weeks after Pace opened its new Chelsea headquarters. The hire mirrored Glimcher’s ambitions at the time. Pace wasn’t simply growing its footprint—it was trying to reinvent itself. The gallery wanted a stronger editorial voice, a broader public profile, and a brand that felt less like an old-school dealership and more like a cultural institution.

Over the next six years, Redgrift was instrumental to that strategy. She led the gallery’s communications through the pandemic and oversaw campaigns for projects ranging from the Don Marron collection coup with Gagosian and Acquavella to the multipart partnership with Institut Restellini and the launch of Pace DiDonna Schrader. She worked on the gallery’s expansion into new markets, including Seoul, Tokyo, London, Palm Beach, and East Hampton.

“I feel privileged to have been part of this storied gallery and to have had the opportunity to shape Pace’s evolution with Marc and Sam,” Redgrift told ARTnews, referring to Samanthe Rubell, the gallery’s president. “It has been a very special experience to work closely with Arne and so many wonderful artists and colleagues over the past seven years.” (Marc’s father, Arne Glimcher, is the gallery’s founder and chairman.)

Glimcher was equally warm about Redgrift’s departure, telling ARTnews that she “helped build and define the culture of Pace over her tenure and will be greatly missed.”

Forest Brandi’s trajectory was just as notable. Arriving at the gallery after a stint as executive assistant at Marian Goodman gallery, she started as Glimcher’s executive assistant, became his chief of staff, then made the jump into sales, eventually rising to senior sales director.

“Dani has also been a great and dynamic member of Pace’s team and made a strong impact over the last eight years,” Glimcher said. “We’re excited to continue to work with her in a new capacity which will soon be announced.”

The two careers often ran in parallel. In 2021, after Pace’s leadership was reshuffled following an investigation into workplace culture, both received major promotions. Redgrift became chief communications and marketing officer, while Forest was elevated to chief of staff as the gallery unveiled a new executive structure. At that time, senior director Samanthe Rubell and Joe Baptista, the gallery’s vice president, were tapped to lead the sales team. Rubell was named president in 2022, while Baptista, who eventually became a partner, left the gallery in 2025 and started the Equivalence Art Agency. Jessie Washburne-Harris, who joined Pace as vice president in 2021, left the gallery in 2025 for White Cube, though she left her post there earlier this month.

In 2021, Pace was hiring, opening new locations, experimenting with Web3, launching ambitious public programming, and investing heavily in departments that reached far beyond selling art. Today, the picture looks very different.

The communications operation has been drastically reduced following multiple rounds of layoffs, though it’s unclear to what extent. Exactly where Redgrift and Forest will surface next remains to be seen.

item.title: New French Law Sparks Hope for Long-Awaited Return of Looted ‘Ségou Treasure’ to Senegal - ARTnews.com
item.description:
For decades, the descendants of the Senegalese Muslim mystic, scholar, and military commander Omar Saïdou Tall have been trying to retrieve his stolen belongings, known as the “treasure of Ségou,” from the French state.

The trove, spread across several French museums and the national library, includes nearly 500 manuscripts containing Tall’s writings and those of contemporaries documenting the region’s history and culture, plus jewelry, weapons, and other artifacts. In 1890, French troops led by General Louis Archinard snatched them from Tall’s family palace, located in the town of Ségou, in today’s Mali.

To many in Senegal, who remember Tall as an anti-colonial hero and founder of the 19th-century Toucouleur empire, which covered present-day Senegal, Mali, and Guinea, the pillaged items are a precious, missing part of their heritage.

Now, thanks to a new French law facilitating the restitution of looted colonial-era artifacts, Tall’s heirs in Senegal are hoping the Ségou treasure will finally come home, according to a report by Le Monde. “That’s my mission,” said Thierno Madani Tall, an influential Muslim religious figure in Dakar, and a direct descendant of the 19th-century leader. “This law is essential, because words have been said,” Madani Tall told Le Monde. “France is finally acknowledging that it stole these highly valuable objects. They have been well preserved, but it’s time for them to come home.”

Cultural artifacts were not the only things taken during the French raid of Ségou. In 1995, France repatriated the remains of Tall’s grandson, Abdoulaye Tall, who was kidnapped during the same 1890 attack. The boy was 10 years old at the time and was brought back to France, where he was forced to assimilate and live with a wealthy family in Paris. He later became the first African student accepted into the prestigious Saint-Cyr French military school. His life was cut short at age 20, however, when he died of an illness.

In 2019, France also returned Tall’s sword, which had been part of the Ségou treasure.

Yet those isolated cases were the result of years of cumbersome diplomacy and legislation. By contrast, the historic law adopted in May was designed to simplify the return of items like the Ségou treasure — marking a landmark reform in President Emmanuel Macron’s effort to ease France’s tense relationship with its former colonies, while reckoning with its painful colonial past.

The new law also helped fulfill Macron’s 2017 promise to return African heritage to the continent, becoming the last of three so-called “framework” laws designed to ease the return of cultural objects owned by the French state. While the two other framework laws apply separately to human remains and Nazi-looted art, this last one concerns items looted from 1815 to 1972, during the time of France’s second colonial empire, up until the UNESCO World Heritage Convention. However, the law avoids explicit mention of colonialism, effectively broadening its scope.

Once an official restitution request is made for the Ségou treasure – in this case by Senegal — then two committees, including experts from France and the requesting country, plus government representatives, will examine the case. Officials in Senegal told Le Monde they plan to lodge a formal request following their completion of a full inventory. In the meantime, French curators are working on digitizing the Ségou treasure manuscripts for study anywhere in the world.

item.title: The Artist Mapping Knoxville’s Art Scene With Wood and Wire - Hyperallergic
item.description:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. — On the first Friday of each month, a dozen or more exhibitions open across galleries, studios, and temporary spaces in Knoxville. For many people in the small city’s art community, the night is either an overwhelming jumble or a repetitive routine. Artist Lauren Farkas’s maps offer a way through.

“If everything is on the map, people get overwhelmed,” Farkas told Hyperallergic. “I put all the things that I would like to go to if I had enough time on the map.”

Farkas, a high school art teacher at L&N STEM Academy who has lived in Knoxville for nine years, said that she considers her educational work to be “a long-form performance piece.” She approaches each map as an artwork with a similar sense of structure: The geography remains fixed, while the shows and events shift from month to month.

Anchored by the Knoxville Museum of Art (KMA) and the University of Tennessee School of Art, the city's arts ecosystem extends beyond downtown’s familiar gallery circuit to include a growing network of artist-run spaces, community studios, and exhibitions that many attendees might otherwise overlook.

Farkas has used watercolor, tape, and digital animation, among other forms, to craft First Friday maps that help people make sense of the evening’s many possibilities — and feel confident exploring them.

 “It’s an invitation, especially for people who might not otherwise feel they belong in those spaces,” Farkas explained.

One map transformed a pair of white sneakers into a walking guide, with Knoxville’s streets and gallery locations etched directly into the soles so that each step echoed the idea of an “art walk.” Another was made entirely from locally harvested materials — paper mulberry pulp, goldenrod, black walnut ink, acorns, and charred wood — creating, as Farkas describes it, “a map of the place with the place.”

For Kelsie Conley, assistant curator at the KMA, the maps transcend the role of an ordinary event guide. “They slow us down and change the way we experience the city,” she said. “They still do the practical work of helping us move through the city, but the information becomes something you have to spend time with. They ask us to think about the city as something that is felt, rather than just a fixed collection of destinations.”

The maps began as a way to orient Farkas herself in the city’s vibrant arts scene. Three years ago, she was sitting at her desk, scrolling through her phone, and making a plan for the evening. She sketched a map for herself in colored pencil — an attempt to make sense of First Fridays and get to as many shows as possible, thinking her way through time and space. She shared it on her Instagram story. A few friends started referencing it, and a project took shape.

“It was useful for me, and someone else used it,” Farkas said. “I thought, ‘Maybe that’s a need or a deficit in the local art world here.’”

Farkas continued creating simple maps over the next few months, posting them to her Instagram story. Around month four or five, she tried using different materials — watercolors led to markers, embroidery, wood ash, gouache on vellum, and even a double-sided shadow lamp.

Her audience is not easy to track, and she doesn’t always know who is using the maps. Some follow along through her Substack; others may just learn about her work through word of mouth.

The maps have already changed how people experience First Friday; Conley also credits them with flattening the boundaries within Knoxville’s art scene. “There’s no hierarchy to them,” she said. Whether it’s an exhibition at a major gallery or in someone’s apartment, Farkas treats them as equally worthy of attention. 

Artist Josh Shorey describes First Friday as “a tradition and a distributed network” — a monthly event that has evolved organically, without a central organizing body. When a photographer who had recently moved to Knoxville from Los Angeles asked him how First Friday worked, Shorey found himself pulling up one of Farkas’s maps to explain it.

“Doing this for every First Friday builds a culture,” said Farkas. “It helps build consistency. I want people to see the value and interconnectedness of everything happening on First Friday.”

item.title: A New Book Celebrates More Than 250 Trailblazing Women Photographers Across 200 Years - Colossal
item.description:
In the introduction of a new book titled Great Women Photographers, Fiona Rogers writes, “If ‘greatness’ has long been defined by visibility and remembrance, then the continued documentation and celebration of women’s photographic practice is not only relevant but essential.”

The forthcoming title spans a multitude of photographic works from 68 countries and covers nearly 200 years of history. It’s the fourth volume in Phaidon’s series of books commemorating influential women in the artistic sphere, with previous installments focusing on distinct creative mediums such as painting and sculpting.

Highlighting more than 250 women in the field of photography, Great Women Photographers is organized alphabetically by name. Each artist entry includes recently commissioned texts written by leading scholars, accompanied with iconic images from the featured photographers.

From photojournalism and editorial portraiture to cameraless images and conceptual landscapes, Great Women Photographers is not only a visual record of the diverse contributions made by women but also, as the publisher notes, “a new lens on the world, inviting readers to discover, engage with, and be inspired by the work of some of the world’s greatest image-makers.”

You may also enjoy exploring other titles in the series, including Great Women Artists, Great Women Painters, and Great Women Sculptors. item.title: Michael E. Smith, the Elusive Sculptor-Poet, Opens Up After a Decade of Dodging Interviews - ARTnews.com
item.description:
When I learned of an opportunity to interview Michael E. Smith—an artist I’ve long admired—my brain boomeranged: I was excited to hear from an elusive artist who seldom speaks, but also stumped as to what exactly I might ask the man. I intuited that direct questions—of the what does this mean, why did you make that variety—wouldn’t do for an artist whose work is so withholding. His sculptures have this magical yet vernacular quality you’d feel silly overexplaining.

Smith’s work—characterized by playful arrangements of found objects—elides language … or so I thought. So often, what makes an artwork great is also what makes my job as a writer hard.

Yet after making the trek to Mass MoCA in the Berkshires, where Smith has a solo show on view through February 21, I realized that his work elides language in part because it has so much in common with it. Smith takes ordinary objects—often readymades—and renders them unfamiliar, both dumber and more mysterious at the same time, in much the way that poets turn the ordinary medium of English on its head. Like a poet, he relies on rhythms and rhymes, and on scrambling semiotics.

Here’s an example: Two long, rolled tubes of yellow paper sit on the floor, greeting viewers to his Mass MoCA show. Immediately, I read them as legs; just as quickly, I wrote off my impulse toward anthropomorphism. Their sole bend, near the end but against the wall, is anything but anatomical. Then, through the door, I glimpsed a set of sticks lying on the ground. This set, wooden with shoes and knees, was indisputably limblike. Only on my way out did I notice the third pair: Two wires hanging from the ceiling are draped over the top of the door, from which they appear to float above, ghostlike. It is through repetition that these pairs come to feel leggier and leggier.

Smith makes you ask: Where does the material end and the metaphor begin? Where do the profound and pedestrian converge, if they do at all?

Other moves feel like puns: Gallery lighting, mounted to the ceiling, is in this show unplugged, cords dangling and cans unscrewed. Here what we call “light” feels jarringly heavy as it sags. I’m told that visitors keep walking right into the dangling plugs, so used we are to tuning out the fixtures from our field of view.

As with any artist whose work has been subject to the machinations of language, there are the narrative tropes that will haunt him for life—the Detroit-born-artist-working-with-post-industrial-refuse story. He has, however, been living in New England for decades,and such a story does little to convey the experience of encountering his work. Fair enough: It’s hard to write about absence, and he withholds so much. Few works in the show are titled, boxes filled with objects remain closed (one is even tightly wrapped in cellophane), and canvases are stacked one atop the other like pizza boxes—content and images concealed.

After much mulling (and an illicit-feeling peek inside the boxes and at the paintings), I thought of a few questions for Smith. The artist spoke from his studio in Providence, Rhode Island, where he was between opening shows at Waldo in Maine and at Maxwell Graham in New York.

You haven’t publicly spoken about your work much. Why’s that?

For 10 years I avoided doing interviews, but I’m actually weirdly super talkative if you get me going.

I mixed things up for this show, largely becuase I wanted the curator, Emma Poveda, who is a grad student fellow, to have a good experience. I never really collaborate with curators: The process is notoriously dry and empty until install starts, so I just decided it could be interesting if I flipped that inside out and gave Emma complete access. She met my partner and my kids. She spent time here in Providence. She has all our phone numbers. I never let anyone work in my studio for more than two years.

Earlier in my life, I was really disappointed in almost everyone, though there was still 20 percent of the world I absolutely adored and would die for. But it’s flipped now. Weirdly, I feel more connected and in love with humans than I ever have.

I noticed some lists on the stacked canvases at Mass MoCA. What role does list-making play in your work?

I think the origin of the lists is just neurosis. I spend a lot of time on paper, remaking lists of things—even thinking about how to write my materials list in a very truncated way. Rather than saying “stork beak,” it will just say “bird,” and then you have to put together the rest of the bird that’s missing in your head.

The lists are also born from practicalities. I seem to grow into every crevice of what it means to find ways to source meaning … including in the demands that come with making on a professional level, whatever that means. The only shot I have is complete abandon each time. I know that sounds extreme, but at least, if that’s the goal, then how do I negotiate things like shipping and flights and still give myself over all the way? So I just fold everything into the mix. If it’s a part of that day, then it becomes part of the song.

How would you describe your relationship to poetry?

For me, poetry is related to songwriting, and I’ve read more poetry than anything else. To me, the best word for talking about the indescribable aspects of what makes something work is often “poetic.” I’ve never studied writing or the theory of it, so maybe this is a common way to think about it, but for me there’s no other art form that separates itself from its use or function quite like poetry. A poem seems to be beyond writing somehow.

I love the idea of a poet being the most lightweight of all—even lighter than the troubadour. All they need to work is a piece of burnt wood, if that; they can also just rely on memory.

This show had these rhyming and rhythm moments that really made me think of the structure of the show as poem-like.

Totally. I live in music, especially pop music. Sometimes, I build shows around certain artists or a suite of songs that somehow holds what I’m feeling or what’s happening. Music gives me a way in.

The last work in the Mass MoCA show, titled More Bounce (2026), is a reference to a Zapp song, “More Bounce to the Ounce.” I think that song is asking us all to be more rubber and keep bouncing to survive. Sound is in the work a lot, and rhythm for sure. Rhythm is the material I’m working with.

How do you go about choosing what objects to work with? When you see something, do you know right away what it will be?

Things choose me. I don’t know if it’s a blessing or a curse, but the schedule I keep feels like the blue-collar response to having two teenagers and trying to keep my promise to my partner: We’ve worked so hard to try not to give any energy to anything we don’t believe in. It seemed like a pipe dream in the beginning, but we did it for a while. A lot of times, the materials were because we didn’t have a ton of money.

I remember when I was in the Venice Biennale [in 2019], and they gave me the Scarpa Garden. I thought: Lord have mercy. I did a site visit. I try to do that as little as possible, but in this case, I had to. It was nothing, nothing, no ideas. The show was getting close, and every morning I’d wake up with panic. Like, how do I live up to this incredible opportunity, in maybe the best spot you could possibly have? I’m not used to that. Usually, people put me in the corner, or I’m weird shit in the stairwell.

I didn’t have funds. In the beginning, I refused advances, because I don’t want to owe people money. But that Christmas, my son got an anvil from my father-in-law, who’s a blacksmith and a glassblower. Boom: The whole idea was there. We ordered anvils from throughout Europe, from different ages. They could be outside. People could sit on them. They’re heavy as shit.

A lot of times it’s like that. That one’s very clean. But so much of what I do feels like being a spiritual detective or something, yet I try to be as pragmatic as possible. Free things, or Craigslist free … if you can find something that motivates you outside of the unbearable lightness of trying to do something worth your time, then just jump. We bleed for it and hopefully people dig it.

That’s also where the work feels like poetry to me. Poets take language—this very pedestrian, perfunctory material—and strip it down while also turning it into something greater than the sum of its parts. The iPhone boxes do that for me; they just felt so unfamiliar and special in a way that I hadn’t thought about before.

That’s what I’m looking for, some kind of nexus where all the different forms of our understanding and consciousness are firing, like many memories and many layers of information all at once. It’s like you can see something in a different way for a minute if you’re in it, and that’s generally durational and maybe even immersive. You have to give over.

That’s part of the reason I build shows the way I do. I was always annoyed with the way attendance works at an exhibition. Anywhere else … you would never listen to six songs simultaneously. It’s just such a stale way to experience something so powerful. We made a fake band when I was in undergrad for that reason, so that people would come and act as though they were at a show—much more relaxed.

Totally. Is that how you landed on the car wash next to Mass MoCA as a kind of motif, and as a site for an artwork and performance?

I was really into the car wash right away. It made me think of Ed Ruscha, and of my grandfather, who worked at Hydramatic, a factory in Detroit. Half of my family worked in the factories, and my grandfather loved washing cars. He worked most of his life to get a Cadillac, and then he never drove it. He would just pull it out, wash it, put it back.

Cars were of almost religious importance in our family. That wasn’t important for the show, but I know from experience that if I connect to a material on a personal level, beneath that will be something universal. It’s just a good fuel for me, and the space’s little weird stalls felt kind of like little galleries or something. I can be impulsive with initial decisions, and then it’s like, “Oh fuck! Now, how do I make this work?” I got a lot of heart, but if I had to figure it out first and then do it, I’d never do anything.

You also collaborate with your kids a lot.

They’ve always been a part of all of it; it just felt very natural. I did this series of events at Giorno Poetry Systems, and my daughter performed, which was super cool. My son drives through sketchbooks at a ridiculous pace, to the point where I feel like we’re killing some trees. I brought in a huge stack of them, and everybody got to flip through them, which they were into. I explained to my son, they’re still yours, but if I were to frame them as an artwork, it’s a window into your head. To look at a 15-year-old’s sketchbook is a powerful experience for a person who’s in their 30s or 40s. I asked: Are you okay with this? Is there anything you would want to get rid of? He said nah, it’s cool; it’s all good.

And then sometimes I put them to work just like good old-fashioned child labor! [Laughs] They like it though; we hang out. They have different skills. My son is like drunken style, so if I’m stuck on something, he’ll just plow through. My daughter is just incredible with color mixing, patterns, repetition … she’s got more of a painter’s mind and sensitivity to stuff. I also work with a partner, Scott. I don’t call anyone assistants. I usually work with young artists and I pay them whatever I can afford to, and we learn from each other. That’s worked pretty well, surprisingly.

I have this strong, strong pull to at least just walk gracefully, whatever the fuck that means—to be as harmless as possible while all of this happens.

It sounds like the lifestyle and the art are supporting each other. 

Yeah. If anything takes the hit, it’s the life part. But we’re fighting for the way we want to live. It can seem almost pointless, though it feels like a perfect time for work like mine, because any attempt at reasoning or objective thought seems laughable in the face of all that spirals around us.

And I mean, what’s the alternative? It’s not like there are a lot of attractive things that I’m missing out on.

A friend once described being an artist as “the best job I’ve ever had”—meaning, the least soul sucking way to spend one‘s time and energy—which I think about a lot.

One of my favorite songs is Son House’s Preachin’ the Blues  (1930). My favorite line is, “I’m gonna join the Baptist Church … so I won’t have to work.” I know that to a lot of people, that sounds lazy or whatever. But no, having a job is an oppressive experience for 99.9% of the planet.

I don’t mind working. I don’t want to have a job.

David Graeber’s book Bullshit Jobs makes the argument that capitalism hurts rich people and poor people alike because it forces us to spend our time on pointless and soulless things, pursuing anything but truth and beauty and kindness.

And it sets up enemies immediately, as if everyone is competing to collect acorns. It took me so long to get rid of that basal impulse. I‘ll never forget when I did this New York studio program thing, and this artist named Mike Dopp was listening to me and my homie talk about art. We were talking about it like it was sports. Being from Detroit, we felt like underdogs, like we shouldn’t have even been there. He had the courage to pop around and school us on how art isn’t competitive, and I feel so lucky to have glimpsed maybe a bit of peace in terms of acceptance.

That’s why I keep coming back to that word “harmless.” I think it is about the best I can come up with these days. Art has introduced me to so much complexity. The amount of arrogance it would take at this point for me to profess understanding or any judgment whatsoever … At best, I try not to do any harm, and if I get there, that’s pretty cool.

item.title: Fried at Last: Why Michael Fried’s Attacks on Literalism Matter As Never Before - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Finally! The real Michael Fried has stood up. A new collection of his life’s work reveals him to be a poet with a memory bestowed from the gods—one who weathered Peter Schjeldahl’s trumped-up charges of being a formalist, conservative fuddy-dud, one who emerges in our AI slop epoch as one of the great art seers who makes a frightening lot of sense, now more than ever. The critic who found a helpful narrative to understand the history, and future, of our images, without a drop of cynicism. This lefty aesthete salutes you!

The 87-year-old American critic is more than a mere Judd-Serra-Andre hater who wouldn’t be caught dead at Oh, Mary! on Broadway. The proof is Bloomsbury’s new box set of his collected writings—critical essays, yes, but especially his beautifully mundane, revelatory prose-poems, and a book-length interview with himself (a sort of intellectual autobiography). Collected Writings: Essays, Poems, Interviews (2026) is the big sum-up, a crown jewel of Fried’s life work, extending the rigor of his still-polemical “Art and Objecthood” (1967), the Artforum essay that confirmed his notoriety. That essay (deservedly) took the piss out of the then-nascent, post-Warhol scene of po-faced “Minimalists”; Fried chided the group for their literalness and theatricality.

Theater kids: don’t sharpen your Our Town pitchforks yet. Fried’s not knocking all theater. In truth, he’s more of a dirty old Brechtian with no use for art-as-mindless-entertainment. He’s against narcissistic theatricality concerned only with the “I,” with whether ironic gags and verbal aperçus will get an arch laugh. Fried has been falsely pegged as a Hilton Kramer lame-o defending some staid, starch-filled idea of art history: Manet good, Judd bad, old pretty art good, new weird art bad. No, goddamnit! Slow down, read closely. For Fried is, as his poems prove, a writer attuned to the shape of thought and the sound of a word. He is the last of a dying breed (but they’ll come back): the gentle critic with the chapeau—amiable, digressive, and slow in the wind-up, like Henry James in lit-crit mode. Fried is also for a lot of things. He is a stealth optimist.

What Fried really wants out of his attacks on theatricality, as becomes clear through a slow reading of both the Collected Writings, is for us to reject the kneejerk modern mandate to accept whatever we, the audience, are trained to want by markets, trends, and consumerist-bourgeois society. Turning to memories of Edward Said, Franz Kafka’s Diaries, and Shakespeare’s Coriolanus, he poetically expresses his moral outrage at the Israeli genocide of the Palestinians: “no thoughts of halcyon younger days can hold our long against present horrors.” And in a moving obituary to the late sculptor Anthony Caro, his lifelong friend, Fried speaks passionately: “I felt that fireworks should have been set off [for Caro’s Gagosian show in 2013], prisoners reprieved, travel made gratis, a bank holiday declared—something spectacularly out of the ordinary ought to have been arranged to mark so extraordinary an achievement.” Fried articulates a preference for artists who make absorbing works, works in conversation with good (i.e., mystery-stoking) art that came before it. Fried’s artists (Caro, as well as Kenneth Noland, Jeff Wall, Douglas Gordon, and Philippe Parreno) are hectic beavers, go-for-brokers who don’t care whether they will receive a positive review in the Times or make a big splashy wow at Whitney-Venice-MoMA. They are too concerned with their own intense endeavors to heed the latest vogue.

This is what I take Fried to mean when he says “absorption”: you, the audience, are drawn more deeply into beholding something that pulls you into its ornery, meditative orbit instead of meeting you where you already are. Art remains its own harmonizing, mystical thing, separate from you. Absorptive art beckons the viewer—who chases after that which ignores it, a tale as old as time—whereas the Minimalism Fried attacked was very big, very look-at-me, very exhibitionist. Its absorption was painfully literal: Step right up, folks, finish the artwork by moving through it yourself! Maybe finish art history while you’re at it! It all culminates in one person: YOU, the 2006 Time Person of the Year! Art doesn’t exist until YOU—the big American “I”—walk up and start making it exist.

Lies! Fried fights a good fight against such solipsistic falsities. He is like an activist who has, for sixty years now, chained himself to a tree, the mighty oak of Modernism, refusing to let Literalism’s bulldozers pass. The tree has been around since 1759. It is old, sure, but lovely, sturdy, centering; it still provides shade. And the Diderot-Baudelaire-Fried tree abides even as the forest burns mutely round it, match lit by Elon Musk and company. We need Fried as never before to deal with a world deluged by the hellish convenience of AI, whose so-called art takes even literalism too literally.

Fried combs through the tangled past to critique the present with “conviction,” a pet word of his. A critic with conviction takes bets on what in her era will last, guided by Baudelaire’s evergreen missive, as Fried notes in an essay on the poet-critic, that criticism must be “partial, passionate, and political.” “Never before” is a phrase that recurs throughout his criticism. Never before Manet’s Olympia or Luncheon on the Grass (both 1863) had anyone so strikingly frozen the viewer with a confrontational “facingness”—the nude woman now stares back at you, the male patron, but you will never know what is in her gaze. Never before Anthony Caro (and, as we learn, never before Caro’s conversation with Fried specifically) had anyone rendered smallness as an abstract idea in itself; rather it was figured as a scaled-down bigness.

Fried is constantly surprised. This “never before”-ness has political implications: it suggests that art history is unfixed and malleable, and that it contains problems awaiting someone with Fried’s eagle eye to spot them, to survey the scene and intervene with conviction in the mess of histories. How anyone ever saw Fried as a holier-than-thou aristocratic formalist is beyond me. Maybe people didn’t read him closely. Or maybe he needed a social media manager.

The Buñuelian skeptic in me also shirks at Fried’s approving references to Diderot’s petite église invisible, the small hidden church whose members—painters, critics, curators, patrons—are the vision-gifted serious pursuers of art history. This still seems to presume one mega-history, one scripture. But Fried’s thought is far too varied and weird—closer to Manny Farber’s than Clement Greenberg’s—to permit dogmatic religiosity for long. (Fried read Greenberg closely, but he is hardly a worshipper of that self-appointed judge with his narrow docket of good and bad objects.) Just as Caro’s small table sculptures—which suggest the ground but never touch it, their sole sculptural curves dipping just below—retain their politically rebellious smallness, so, too, does Fried’s criticism suggest the bottom of religion without finding it.

Fried practices art history and criticism as a poetic, almost magical endeavor. “The medium of the prose poem is thought,” Fried writes in “The Prose Poem,” a veritable manifesto on his own process. The simple magic consists of following a thought meticulously through; finding, as its rope nears an end, another thread; and then following that thread ad infinitum, until one turns back to regard the cluster of rich, powerful, pristine ideas that have emerged. The idea is one of extension, of continuing the thread of modernity, of constantly making new again and again—maintaining continuity against so many distractions, ignoring the jewelry-rattlers who want to be entertained in the fancy theatah.

item.title: Egyptian Archaeologists Uncover Three Ancient Tombs at Bahariya Oasis - ARTnews.com
item.description:
An Egyptian archaeological mission has discovered three tombs from different historical periods at the Sheikh Sobi archaeological site in the Bahariya Oasis. The news was reported by several outlets, including Arab News, following an announcement by Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.

The site, which lies about 225 miles southwest of Giza, contains a necropolis used to bury governors and priests of the oasis during Egypt’s Late Period (664–332 BCE), as well as the Bawiti Temple, built during the 26th dynasty (664–525 BCE) in honor of the pharaoh Ahmose II, the last great native pharaoh before the Persian conquest of Egypt.

The newly discovered burial structures consist of a rock-cut family tomb containing five Late Period mummies, a Roman-period tomb in a stairwell-style design, and a third tomb, also dating to the Roman era, built around a burial shaft. Sabri Farag, director general of antiquities at the Bahariya Oasis and head of the mission, told Arab News that the 40-member mission, comprising archaeologists and other workers, had been excavating at the site for three months before the tombs were discovered.

The first tomb features a square shaft about 10 feet deep leading to two burial chambers. In the western chamber, archaeologists found a limestone sarcophagus containing a mummy wrapped in linen bandages. A larger northern chamber hosted four additional limestone sarcophagi holding linen-wrapped mummies, indicating that the tomb was used by members of the same family.

The second tomb consists of a staircase leading into a chamber. The lack of funerary decoration suggests that this chamber was never used for an actual burial. The third tomb consists of a rectangular well leading to a small hall or reception area believed to have been used to prepare mummies for burial. Two connected chambers contained fragments of sarcophagi.

Additional artifacts recovered during the excavation included pottery vessels, flasks, plates and offering tables made of limestone and sandstone. 

The team also recovered small terracotta votive figurines depicting maternal figures and stylized animals.

Egyptologist Dr. Hassan Selim told Arab News that artifacts from the site had a distinctive artistic character and noted that local artists did not always adhere to traditional ancient Egyptian styles. Instead, he noted, they revealed details about the daily life and religious beliefs in the region.

item.title: A New Video Game is Subverting the Secrecy of Michael Heizer’s ’City’ - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Tulsa, Oklahoma-based digital artist Lily Belmira has made a new, free video game allowing anyone to virtually visit Michael Heizer’s mysterious and radically difficult-to-enter land artwork in the Nevada desert, titled City. Only six people a day who are willing to pay the regular admission fee of $150 are permitted to explore City, one of the world’s largest artworks, in person. Spanning over a mile and a half, its precise location has been kept secret to some degree since its opening in 2022.

But Belmira hopes to offer a virtual way around all that, while deliberately challenging the notion of restricted access to art, in favor of a more democratic and broad-reaching approach.

She told ARTnews via email that she made the video game out of “a genuine interest in showing City to more people.” But it is also a critique of what she calls a “bourgeois scar on the earth,” albeit a “beautiful” one, in an artist statement. “I didn’t like City when I started, and I saw this project as a way to undermine its power,” she adds.

To that end, players of Belmira’s City by Michael Heizer [Free Version], which anyone can try by clicking here, must start behind an intentionally obtrusive no-trespassing fence. An opening further along the fence eventually allows users to wander through a simulation of Heizer’s barren, manicured landscape of paths, mounds, and depressions, where strange, abstract geometric sculptures emerge, appearing equally ancient and futuristic, or alien. Belmira used LIDAR data available online to model City’s terrain, as well as Google Maps satellite imagery.  

While she feels the video game “is forgiving [Heizer] in some way,” Belmira told ARTnews she still wonders: “How can an artwork that has been seen by so few people have so much power?” She points to City’s “aura” and role in securing the surrounding land as a national monument by 2015 executive order. “The game asks if bringing an exclusive artwork down to the level of online art could free the work and its creator from the economic bind that keeps their art from being experienced,” she said.

Dubbed the art-world Atlantis, City took some 50 years to make, beginning in the 1970s, and cost $40 million to produce. Like Heizer’s other artworks, often made in remote settings and of epic scope, it has regularly sparked criticism in line with some of Belmira’s views. ARTnews senior editor Alex Greenberger said Heizer’s creations “evince a muscular, macho sensibility.” Others argue the artist’s work reaffirms structures of settler colonialism by omitting Indigenous perspectives of the land being used, as Alicia Harris discussed in a 2020 dissertation.

After virtually strolling through City in Belmira’s video model, some of its mysterious puzzle pieces do, gratifyingly, start to come together. After all, cell phones aren’t allowed on the site, and imagery of the City is limited. We get a better sense of its scale and form, without ever having to trudge through the unforgiving desert heat. Whether Belmira intended it or not, the enjoyable exercise left me curious to experience more, and perhaps, one day, make it there myself.
