item.title: Jewish Digital Cultural Recovery Project Adds AI to Provenance Search Tool - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Jewish Digital Cultural Recovery Project (JDCRP), an organization founded in Berlin in 2016, announced today that it has added AI capabilities to its provenance research tool, Legacy Explorer, which launched last year.

Legacy Explorer is currently able to search five archives, including the Einsatzstab Reichsleiter Rosenberg archive at the Jeu de Paume in Paris, as well as several others that organize property cards and photographs. A sixth archive will be added later this month, according to a statement from the JDCRP.

Prior to this AI sync, users would have to search each archive individually. Now, the AI document-scanning tools, along with partnerships with organizations and archives around the world, will allow researchers to pull information about the same cultural object from different sources at the same time. There are still dozens of other databases and archives for looted artwork and artifacts that contain information about Nazi-looted art and heirlooms.

“The platform addresses an urgent gap in provenance research: the lack of a single place where experts and the general public can easily search across archival collections and access the historical documentation of an object’s provenance,” JDCRP board chair Wesley A. Fisher said in a statement about Legacy Explorer. (Fisher is also director of research for the Claims Conference, the nonprofit that co-founded, with the Commission on Art Recovery, JDCRP in 2019.)

Last month, a group of business school professors at Santa Clara University launched a new AI tool aimed at helping heirs research and identify Nazi-era looted artwork by scraping the Jeu de Paume–managed database managed.

“For descendants of survivors, Legacy Explorer’s expansion will provide a path to trace the journey of cultural property stolen from their families,” said Deirdre Berger, the chair of JDCRP’s executive board.

item.title: Before France Approved Bayeux Tapestry Loan, a British Official Had To ‘Get On His Knees and Propose’ - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Bayeux Tapestry is set for its big moment at the British Museum this fall, but the New York Times is dishing on how the loan came to be.

In a feature published Tuesday, reporter Alex Marshall reveals the many behind-the-scenes negotiations that brought the famed Romanesque-style textile artwork depicting the 1066 Norman invasion back home to the UK.

The most recent loan request was far from the first: the UK had previously asked for the work in 1953, 1966, and 1980. So what changed? As Marshall tells it, Chris Bryant, a senior UK official, went to the Cannes Film Festival last year to meet with Rachida Dati, France’s then–culture minister. (Dati, a controversial figure for her right-wing views, stepped down in February to run for mayor of Paris.) At Cannes, Dati arrived 25 minutes late to a 30-minute meeting, at which point she told Bryant that she had good news on the tapestry, but that he had to, in Marshall’s words, “get on his knees and propose.”

“I said, ‘I’ve already got a husband,'” Bryant told the Times. “So do I,” Dati replied, according to Bryant. “What’s wrong with polyamory?”

Bryant said he did get down on one knee. Several weeks later, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the loan agreement at the British Museum.

Bryant’s telling is hardly the triumphal story that the Brits would no doubt like to spin. But, hey, a win is a win.

The tapestry is set to go on view from September 2026 to July 2027, and tickets for the exhibition are already sold out through December. Additional tickets will go on sale in October and January. The British Museum has said it anticipates it will be one of the most visited exhibitions in the institution’s two-and-a-half-century history.

item.title: Six Films on Art and Resistance at BlackStar Film Festival - Hyperallergic
item.description:
PHILADELPHIA — Held from August 6 to 9, the BlackStar Film Festival marked its 15th anniversary this year with 91 films underscoring its ongoing commitment to “a cinema for liberation.” That vision is one of collective endurance, a shared struggle rooted in solidarity and dogged determination. It suffused Haile Gerima’s Black Lions, Roman Wolves, a five-part documentary on Ethiopia’s resistance to the Italian invasion of 1935; artist Suneil Sanzgiri’s “An Impossible Address,” a poetic documentary on the legacy of Indian and African freedom struggles against Portuguese colonialism; and Harlan Banks’s “I Wonder Shall I Fly,” weaving Black diasporic footage with precious 1940s recordings of interviews with formerly enslaved people.

It also permeated the panels and joyful gatherings that bind BlackStar’s mission to its practice of building an ecosystem for independent and experimental film workers, artists, and writers beyond the market. We selected a few favorites from the festival that deepened our experience of visual art and brought the fight for a just world into view.

A Life in Art: Through the Eye of Dr. Leslie King Hammond (2026), dir. Ben Baker-Lee and Rassaan Hammond

When art historian, critic, and artist Dr. Leslie King Hammond was a child, one of her eyes had to be removed. She recalls the transformative experience of watching a glassblower create her artificial eye. The glassblower’s ability to shape raw material into something intricate and lifelike captivated her. That fascination never left her, leading to a lifelong dedication to the arts.

It’s a fitting origin story for Hammond, who has spent her career teaching others how to see work by artists of color with greater clarity and precision. A Life in Art: Through the Eye of Dr. Leslie King Hammond, directed by Ben Baker-Lee and Rassaan Hammond, her son, pays tribute to these efforts. Hammond has taught and mentored numerous artists, including Ernest Shaw, Jeffrey Kent, and Amy Sherald. In one scene, we see Hammond in the studio with Sherald as she paints Michelle Obama’s portrait for the National Gallery, the commission that catapulted her to fame. We witness Hammond’s brilliance as she remarks on the painting in progress, her enthusiasm infectious as she contextualizes Sherald’s work. 

Hammond’s approach to criticism is unabashedly honest. In the film, she describes pushing artists to defend their position and articulate their vision so the value of their work isn’t diminished or misunderstood. At heart is a desire to help them articulate “the meat of the journey of [their] lives.” Interactions with family, peers, and friends reveal that joy, humor, and care are integral to Hammond’s practice, just as vital as the rigor with which she writes and speaks about art. Her friendships with artist Joyce J. Scott and fellow curator Lowery Stokes Sims are a delight to behold. —Elodie Saint-Louis

Aanikoobijigan [ancestor / great-grandparent / great-grandchild] (2026), dir. Adam and Zack Khalil

In the bowels of the Michigan State University (MSU) football stadium, as games rage on and fans roar, ancestors were forced to lie in wait. That haunting scene is captured in one of many indelible sequences in Aanikoobijigan, an experimental collage of documentary and video art directed by brothers Adam and Zack Khalil (Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians). The film traces the Michigan Anishinaabek Cultural Preservation and Repatriation Alliance’s (MACPRA) years-long efforts to bring home the stolen remains of hundreds of Anishinaabe ancestors held by the MSU Museum. The result is a poignant, creative homage to the organizers who held the university accountable, to the ancestors themselves, and to the ongoing fight to repair the colonial violence still inflicted by museums today.

Rejecting the traditional documentary form, Adam and Zack Khalil capture the depth of this specific repatriation case by weaving together interviews with MACPRA officers and Native leaders; the colonial history of museums and archaeology; and visceral, artistic shots that leave a particularly harrowing residue in the mind's eye. The spirit of the film shines through the voices of outspoken advocates like the late Sydney Martin (Gun Lake Tribe) — a fiery badass who worked as a tribal historic preservation officer and passed away in February of this year — and archaeologist Sonya Atalay (Anishinaabe-Ojibway), who explains the existential threats that non-linear conceptions of time, and relational definitions of selfhood, pose to Western museums.

In the experimental registers, vertiginous shots snake through the sterile environs of archaeological and institutional archives, mimicking the disorientation of burial desecration to remind us that the struggle isn't over yet. The narrator’s provocation from the beginning of the film lingers after the lights go up: “If an object is animate, an archive is a prison. If an object is an Ancestor, when can the grandkids visit?” —Lakshmi Rivera Amin

One More Show (2025), dir. Ahmed Al Danaf and Mai Saad

Words fail in the face of One More Show. The documentary follows five members of the Free Gaza Circus as they navigate displacement and dodge the daily threat of violence under genocide while juggling, beatboxing, and dancing for displaced children and families. Gazan cinematographer Ahmed Al Danaf co-directed the film across borders and internet blackouts with Egypt-based filmmaker Mai Saad, capturing much of the soundscape — children singing, the constant buzz of drones overhead — on a single neck microphone. (All proceeds from the film go directly to the Free Gaza Circus.)

Though Al Danaf and his crew remain behind the camera, their quiet presence and shared grief guide the lens at every turn. Slow, speechless stretches of the film draw our attention to the hum of life in Gaza on the seaside, in the refugee camps, in the markets. The filmmakers record the Free Gaza Circus cooking and conversing as they touch on pain and humor in equal measure. Troupe co-founder Youssef Khedr recalls the bombing that destroyed the circus school he worked so hard to build, clown-in-training Adam Anwar confesses a fear greater than death, and troupe members comfort one another while putting on makeup and fixing bowties before a performance, children’s cheers ringing outside the tent. “Ready to go rogue? And make art?” hollers one member during their pre-clowning huddle. Eighteen years in, the group’s core belief touches each troupe member and child it reaches: Art persists. —Lakshmi Rivera Amin

Bouchra (2025), dir. Orian Barki and Meriem Bennani

Those familiar with 2 LIZARDS, filmmaker Orian Barki and visual artist Meriem Bennani’s viral web series chronicling life in New York during the COVID-19 lockdown, will recognize elements of its idiosyncratic universe in Bouchra, the duo’s debut feature. Like 2 Lizards, Bouchra draws from Bennani’s personal experience and features a cast of anthropomorphic animals. The film’s protagonist is the titular Bouchra, an endearing Moroccan filmmaker who has been estranged from her mother, Aicha, after coming out to her in a letter. A sojourn back home offers an opportunity to address the rift between them, and Bouchra begins making a film about her relationship with her mother. Their conversations, full of tenderness and humor, are the film’s emotional engine. 

A film within a film, Bouchra shifts back and forth from Bouchra’s process of making the film and the actual film she ends up creating. Barki and Bennani complicate this structure in the closing sequence, in which Aicha and a lively group of actresses rehearse one of the earlier scenes. Shot in a documentary style, the sequence adds yet another layer to the film. Sexy, formally inventive, and poignant, Bouchra is a must-see. —Elodie Saint-Louis

La West Side Familia (2026), dir. Taylor Hosking

We’ve all seen the Upper West Side of movies and pop culture: liberal, affluent, predominantly White. But at 93rd Street and Columbus Avenue, La West Side Familia has been advocating for the local Puerto Rican community’s rights for over half a century. Founder Chino Familia is one of the pivotal figures at the center of this documentary by journalist and first-time filmmaker Taylor Hosking, who grew up in the same building her late mother was raised in, on the block where the organization was launched.

With La West Side Familia, Hosking braids personal, communal, and political threads to narrate the Puerto Rican history of the neighborhood while processing the loss of her mother during the COVID-19 pandemic. She interviews family members and longtime Nuyoricans who carry memories of the area in the 1970s and ’80s, before the crack epidemic fractured the community and its budding break-dancing and hip-hop circles, and highlights remarkable footage of the local squatters’ rights movement. Chino’s eyes light up as he recounts those early years, from his first protest as a child to his participation in the Puerto Rican independence activists’ 1977 occupation of the Statue of Liberty. George “SEN-One” Morillo, a pioneering graffiti writer, offers us a glimpse into the unbridled world of tagging, even revisiting the abandoned underground Amtrak rails that he and other artists made their own. After the screening on August 7, an emotional Chino got a well-deserved standing ovation and joined the panelists onstage. Though many of his fellow organizers have passed away, this film is a testament to their legacy and the next generation following La Familia’s lead, Hosking among them. —Lakshmi Rivera Amin

Palestine 36 (2025), dir. Annemarie Jacir

Annemarie Jacir’s sweeping historical drama chronicles the Arab Revolt of 1936 to ’39 against British colonial rule, a crucial period in Palestinian history. The film also reveals how the conflict involved a struggle between farmers, dependent on the land for their survival, and members of the Palestinian bourgeoisie, many of whom accommodated the British and turned a blind eye to the mounting catastrophe around them. At the beginning of the film, we meet Yusuf (Karim Daoud Anaya), a young man caught between life in his village Al-Basma and Jerusalem, where he works as a chauffeur for Amir (Dhafer L’Abidine), a wealthy businessman and husband of Khuloud Atef (Yasmine al Massri), a passionate, headstrong journalist who wields her pen to voice Palestinians’ concerns. 

Although Palestine 36 initially appears to center Yusuf, there is no single protagonist. Each character is part of a larger tapestry: dockworker Khaled (Saleh Bakri), whose mistreatment pushes him to join the resistance, and villagers Hanan (Hiam Abbass, excellent as always), Abu Rabab (Kamel El Basha), their widowed daughter Rabab (Yafa Bakri), and granddaughter Afra (Wardi Eilabouni), who resist their displacement as best as they can. Jacir depicts revolt not as a spontaneous achievement of exceptional individuals, but as something that emerges from collective humiliations, losses, and acts of resistance. —Elodie Saint-Louis

item.title: Defying Federal Judge, Kennedy Center Board Votes to Close, Inscribe Trump’s Name on Building - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Thursday to close the center for renovations for a second time, while keeping a smaller, separate theater open.

This week’s vote marked a dramatic escalation in the legal battle over the historic center: the Trump-allied board also moved to inscribe the president’s name beneath the signage—a direct rebuke of a May federal court order that had blocked both the closure and a name change. According to the New York Times, the board has approved an inscription beneath the center’s name reading: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”

The Kennedy Center board voted last December to change the institution’s name to include Trump and to add his name to the marble facade, triggering a financial crisis as performers began dropping from the roster in protest. In the ensuing months, the White House, federal courts, and Washington preservationists have been locked in a legal standoff over where the authority to rename the center lies. Legal experts noted the name change may violate a stipulation established after Congress renamed the center following John F. Kennedy’s assassination in 1963.

US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled on May 29 that the board had acted unlawfully in renaming the institution, finding that only Congress held that power. He also found the board had acted unlawfully in approving a two-year closure for renovations.

Until now, the Trump administration had pursued conventional legal channels to fight the ruling: first a motion in June, which was denied. The President’s name was removed from the facade that month, and scrubbed from the center’s letterhead, website, and other official branding. In July, a federal appeals court denied a bid to restore Trump’s name, finding that the administration had failed to prove the arts complex would be “irreparably injured” by the institution reverting to its original name.

The board’s Thursday resolution reportedly directed officials to pursue “all legal means” to defend what it called President Trump’s rescue of the center “from the brink of disaster.” 

“It is hereby resolved, that the center desires to recognize and honor President Trump’s existential and unprecedented contributions to the survival of the center by all legal means,” the measure said, according to the Times. The meeting was held virtually and not open to the public.

The Kennedy Center, whose chairman has been Trump since February 2025, voted this past March to close the institution for two years for renovations. Judge Cooper blocked the closure, calling it “derelict” for the board to vote without considering the impact on the capital’s leading performing arts institution.

“The board will be expected to prepare itself with sufficient information to make a considered, independent decision,” the judge wrote in May, “taking account of its obligation to both maintain and operate a premiere arts venue and its solemn duty to memorialize a fallen president.”

In response, the president took to social media to berate Judge Cooper as an “anti-Trump hater” and predict that the center would “soon be closed, probably never to open again.” Throughout the case, the institution has argued that removing then restoring the president’s name would waste “time and money” and risk losing donor gifts given only “with the name ‘Trump’ on the building.”  

Judge Cooper is expected to soon review—again—the legality of the latest closure and renaming decisions.

The Kennedy Center has grown increasingly marooned from its many patrons and performing arts peers in recent months, and today has a starkly sparse programming schedule. In January, celebrated composer Philip Glass announced his withdrawal of a symphony honoring Abraham Lincoln that was scheduled for its first-ever performance by the National Symphony Orchestra in June. Meanwhile, the Washington National Opera, which had performed there since 1971, moved out in January, citing low attendance. 

ARTnews has contacted the Kennedy Center for comment.

item.title: The Luxury Industry is Contracting—So Why Are Auction Houses’ Luxury Sales Booming? - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Editor’s Note: This story originally appeared in On Balance, the ARTnews newsletter about the art market and beyond. Sign up here to receive it every Wednesday.

If you’ve been following ARTnews‘ reporting on the luxury market over the last year, you’ll know that luxury sales at the major auction houses are booming. At Christie’s, such sales jumped 30 percent year on year in the first half of 2025, to $468 million, before climbing a further 15 percent, to $539 million, in the first half of this year. Over at Sotheby’s, luxury is even bigger: sales hit a record $2.7 billion in 2025, up 22 percent year on year and accounting for roughly 39 percent of the house’s $7 billion in total sales. That compares with $2.2 billion in luxury sales in 2024 and more than $2 billion in each of the previous two years. 

And this growth is showing no sign of slowing. Sotheby’s reported a record first half for its luxury division in 2026, with global watch sales up 64 percent year on year and jewelry sales up 13 percent. As for Phillips, earlier this year its watch department recorded the most successful spring season in its history, with record-breaking sales across Geneva, New York, and Hong Kong topping $235 million.

However, what makes these numbers appear even more impressive—and perhaps surprising at first glance—is that the broader luxury market has been hemorrhaging buyers. According to consulting firm Bain & Company, 50 million customers exited the market between 2022 and 2024, falling from around 400 million to 350 million. That’s one-eighth of the industry’s buyer base. Bain said this exodus has mostly been driven by soaring prices and a weakening value proposition. In May, the Financial Times‘ Business of Luxury Summit in Puglia similarly painted a picture of a struggling industry, with the CEO of Saint Laurent telling attendees that the industry has to do better at “retaining clients.” Other executives blamed weak consumer sentiment, fragile Chinese demand, and years of aggressive price increases for pushing many shoppers away. 

So why hasn’t this contraction hit the auction houses?

The short answer, according to Max Fawcett, Christie’s global head of jewelry, is that the two markets are not as closely connected as the headline numbers might suggest. Bain’s figures encompass an incredibly broad spectrum of luxury consumption, from $2,000 sneakers and sweaters to high jewelry and watches, while the auction houses tend to operate at the much narrower top end of the market, where wealthy buyers are chasing rare and exceptional objects.

“When we have so many people trying to buy the best things because there are very few of them, it just hasn’t linked through yet from that broader contraction into the auction world,” Fawcett told ARTnews.

Fawcett pointed to what he describes as a “K-shaped recovery,” in which the wealth of the richest consumers has continued to rise even as more discretionary buyers have retreated. That bifurcation is particularly pronounced in jewelry and watches, he said, where the major maisons have continued to report growth. For example, LVMH reported that its watches and jewelry division, which includes Tiffany & Co. and Bulgari, grew 9 percent organically in the first half of 2026 and 11 percent in the second quarter. (Overall revenue at the luxury giant did, however, drop 3 percent on a reported basis in that period.) 

But, of course, this doesn’t mean the two markets are completely separate. Fawcett said Christie’s is seeing some customers who were traditionally primary-market luxury buyers move into auctions after discovering the rarity and value available on the secondary market. Others, namely the ultra-wealthy, are continuing to buy directly from brands despite the premium, drawn by the service, “experiential luxury,” and access that the primary market can offer. 

In other words, the auction houses may not be absorbing the customers who have been lost by the luxury industry. Instead, it looks like they’re benefiting from the same polarization of spending reshaping the primary market. That is, fewer aspirational consumers, but continued—and potentially intensifying—spending by the wealthiest buyers.

The movement from primary to secondary is not necessarily a sign of distress. As Fawcett explained, some clients who once bought predominantly from luxury brands are now turning to Christie’s after discovering that the secondary market can offer rarity, provenance, and, often, a significant price advantage. This can make it more appealing than the primary market.

The distinction made by Fawcett is particularly important in jewelry, where the most desirable stones and pieces can be decades or even centuries old. He pointed to antique jewelry, old-mine emeralds, and Kashmir sapphires (all of which can no longer be produced or mined) as examples of objects for which the secondary market is effectively the primary source.

Price is another draw. Fawcett said a stone bought at auction can sometimes be repolished, reset, and ultimately sold through a luxury maison at a substantial markup. For buyers who are more interested in rarity and the object itself than the experience of buying directly from a brand, auctions can therefore be a more compelling proposition.

But the migration is far from universal, and Fawcett said some of Christie’s wealthiest clients continue to buy directly from the major maisons, even when they know they’re paying a premium. Often, when they do this, they are not simply buying an object, but access to the hyper-exclusive ecosystem around it. This includes private events, world-class service, rubbing shoulders with famous designers and fashion’s top brass, and the status that comes with being one of a brand’s VVIPs.

“It doesn’t matter how much money you have; the auction houses can’t do that most of the time,” Fawcett said of the access offered by the major maisons like Chanel, Cartier, Hermès, and Louis Vuitton.

Sotheby’s, for its part, has been shoring up its luxury experiential offerings. For example, the house has organized ad hoc wine tastings and vineyard tours in France for its VVIP clients. It even embedded some high-end road bike collectors with a Tour de France team in July. The house also recently partnered with high-end, membership-based luxury travel agent Indagare to offer exclusive holidays built around insider cultural access and fine dining. Upcoming trips, which cost around $20,000 per person, include a four-day trip to Venice in September, where guests will stay in the five-star Gritti Palace, tour the Biennale with Sotheby’s managing director for Italy, and visit museums after hours. 

Going back to Fawcett’s comments, it’s therefore not unusual for the same wealthy customer to oscillate between primary and secondary luxury depending on what they’re after—whether it be a new piece and the experience surrounding it from a brand, or an exceptional vintage object that can only be found at auction.

There is also a geographical shift underway, with Christie’s seeing fewer buyers based in Europe, even as many of its sellers remain European. Increasingly, demand is coming from the Middle East, Asia, and the US. This development could become even more significant as European collections accumulated over generations come to market, Fawcett told me.

Luxury is also becoming an important gateway into the auction house ecosystem itself. At Christie’s, 38 percent of new buyers in 2025 made their first purchase through a luxury category rather than art, according to figures previously provided to ARTnews. Many of those purchases were made online, suggesting that luxury can serve as a relatively accessible entry point for clients who might otherwise never have participated in an auction.

Guillaume Cerutti, Christie’s former CEO, previously told ARTnews that luxury sales, alongside contemporary art, had become one of the house’s primary sources of new clients, with the aim of encouraging those buyers to explore other categories, particularly fine art.

Phillips’ results suggest the shift is not confined to Christie’s and Sotheby’s; for its spring season, 40 percent of its buyers were new to the house, with millennials and Gen Zers accounting for nearly a third of bidders and buyers. This shows that the auction houses are not simply harvesting spending from the existing luxury elite—they are also finding ways to bring a new generation of consumers into the secondary market.

Sotheby’s 90 percent sell-through rates for its watches and jewelry sales have helped fuel its record first-half 2026 results for its luxury operation. Josh Pullan, the house’s global head of luxury, said of the results that collectors were responding to “quality, rarity, and provenance.”

As it stands, then, there’s little evidence that the luxury downturn has filtered meaningfully into the auction houses. If anything, the opposite is happening. The houses are capturing spending from wealthy collectors, winning over some former primary-market customers, and using luxury to entice entirely new buyers over to the auction ecosystem.

But that also leaves an important question unanswered. The auction market may be insulated from the loss of aspirational luxury consumers because it is selling to a much narrower and wealthier clientele. If the luxury slowdown eventually reaches that group, however, the relationship between the primary and secondary markets could look very different.

For now, at least, the evidence suggests the auction houses aren’t riding out luxury’s downturn so much as occupying a different, and currently much healthier, part of the market. The question, then, is not whether the luxury downturn will eventually reach the auction houses, but whether they can turn their current divergence from the primary market into a lasting advantage.

item.title: ‘Turn the Volume Up!’ Highlights the History of Speaking Out for Change in America - Colossal
item.description:
From the collection of the Nasher Museum of Art at Duke University, which features a wealth of artwork and artifacts related to social justice and community organizing, a new exhibition highlights American democracy and freedom of speech through the lens of art as an agent of change.

Turn the volume up! includes works by a diverse group of contemporary artists and photographers, from Spider Martin’s dramatic documentation of Freedom Marches during the Civil Rights Movement to Kara Walker’s multimedia interrogations of U.S. history and racial stereotypes. Visitors will also encounter works by the Guerilla Girls, Carrie Mae Weems, Kiki Smith, Bruce Davidson, and many more.

The Nasher has organized the exhibition into five thematic areas: Remarks, Organize, Records, Dissents, and Petitions. Photographs, sculptures, installations, paintings, and more illustrate the array of visual languages artists use to convey important messages, influencing how people discuss issues and are spurred toward civic action.

The Guerilla Girls, for example, famously pasted posters around Manhattan in the 1980s that shone a light on the glaring lack of representation of women artists in not only visual art but across popular culture. Davidson is renowned for illuminating social inequality in visceral photographs, from the Jim Crow South to impoverished neighborhoods in New York City. And Carol Summers’ bold screenprint of a giant red “X” over a photo of a Vietnamese mother and her children was part of a campaign by Artists and Writers Protest urging the end of the war in Vietnam.

Throughout the show’s run, pieces will be rotated in and out so that visitors can experience a wide array of works in the museum’s collection. Turn the volume up! opens on August 27 and will continue through July 11, 2027. Everything Now All at Once also continues through November 1.

item.title: A Picasso Vanished in 1961. The Guggenheim Now Wants It Back - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The Picasso had disappeared without a trace.

On the morning of February 6, 1961, a graduate student and dormitory aide at the University of Pittsburgh reported Picasso's painting "Femme dans un fauteuil" (1918) missing from the Students Union building. The 13.5-by-10.5-inch oil had been on loan from the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation for an exhibition in the fall semester, and was due to be returned to the museum later that month. The school reported the theft to the Pittsburgh Police Department and the FBI was swiftly brought in to investigate, but despite a slew of news articles, notifications to institutions across North America, and a reward for information, the case went cold.

More than six decades later, the Guggenheim says the painting has turned up, and it is headed to court to get it back.

In a lawsuit filed in New York State Supreme Court this week, the Guggenheim Foundation accused Massachusetts residents Lawrence Jay Handler and Wendy Cohen Handler of unlawfully withholding the painting, disregarding the museum's ownership rights, and unjustly benefiting from possessing stolen property.

According to court filings, the Handlers purchased “Femme dans un fauteuil” from Beadleston Fine Art in Manhattan in 1999, nearly 40 years after it went missing in Pittsburgh. But the Guggenheim learned of the painting's reappearance only in July 2023, when a researcher at Christie's who was looking into the work for a private sale consignment brought it to the museum's attention. Collector and mining tycoon Solomon R. Guggenheim, the institution's namesake founder, was listed in the provenance entry for the work in the “Zervos,” Picasso's 1949 catalogue raisonné.

Picasso painted the abstract composition while honeymooning with his first wife, the ballerina Olga Khokhlova, near Biarritz. Guggenheim would acquire the work from London's Gallery Zwemmer in 1936.

It's unclear how the work made its way to the since-shuttered Beadleston gallery on Fifth Avenue, where the Handlers allegedly acquired it. Nor does the lawsuit say whether the Handlers or the gallery were aware of the artwork's provenance. (The gallery's founder, Bill Beadleston, was reportedly among the victims of a $50 million fraud scheme orchestrated by fugitive art dealer Michel Cohen in the early 2000s.)

As soon as it learned of the painting's whereabouts, the Guggenheim moved quickly, sending the owners a formal letter demanding its return in August 2023. That demand was promptly refused, according to court filings. “Femme dans un fauteuil” has remained in limbo at Christie's ever since.

A spokesperson for the Guggenheim told Hyperallergic that it had “attempted to settle the matter with the individuals holding the work.”

“This Picasso, titled 'Femme dans un fauteuil (Woman in an armchair)' (1918), was stolen in 1961 while on loan from the Guggenheim to a university,” the spokesperson said. “The Guggenheim is and always has been the painting’s rightful owner, and we look forward to its recovery.”

Hyperallergic has contacted the Handlers for comment via their attorney at Withers Art and Advisory. Lawrence Jay Handler practices internal medicine and Wendy Cohen Handler is the owner of the private art and jewelry brokerage Estate Treasures, according to the lawsuit. Two unnamed individuals, John Doe and Jane Doe, are also listed as defendants, representing any others who might claim an interest in the painting.

The compact canvas from Picasso's Synthetic Cubist period was valued at $10,000 to $60,000 in 1961, according to the court documents, and is now believed to be worth millions. In filings, the museum requests $3.5 million in compensatory damages, excluding counsel fees, and a declaratory judgment from the court.

Though the Guggenheim received a $7,000 payment from its insurer, Chubb, after the theft in 1961, the museum says it repaid the proceeds in late 2023, following the Christie's discovery, and that Chubb has confirmed the restoration of title to the Guggenheim.

The Guggenheim was previously involved in a different, precedent-setting case over a stolen artwork. In the late 1980s, the museum sought to recover a Chagall gouache that it said was taken from its premises by a mailroom employee two decades earlier. The painting made its way to a Madison Avenue gallery, where it was sold to a couple who displayed it in their living room for years.

When the Guggenheim demanded its return, the defendants argued that they had purchased the gouache in good faith — that they had no reason to believe it had been stolen, and that the museum had waited too long before reporting it missing.

The court eventually ruled that the lawsuit could move forward, cementing New York State as a jurisdiction that tends to protect an artwork's rightful owner, even when the property is acquired by a good-faith buyer. (The two parties eventually settled in 1993.)

“To place the burden of locating stolen artwork on the true owner and to foreclose the rights of that owner to recover its property if the burden is not met would, we believe, encourage illicit trafficking in stolen art,” wrote Chief Judge Solomon Wachtler in a 1991 opinion.

item.title: Long-Misattributed Clara Peeters Still Life Resurfaces After Decades in Storage - Hyperallergic
item.description:
A 17th-century still life that had gathered dust for decades in storage at the National Museum of Norway is set to resurface in a forthcoming exhibition, where it will be publicly attributed to the Flemish painter Clara Peeters for the first time.

Opening October 8, Woman Painter brings "Still Life with small game and grapes on a gilded tazza" (c. 1620) together with the works of 18 other influential yet sometimes overlooked women artists.

Originally attributed to Ambrosius Brueghel, the son of the famed Flemish painter Jan Brueghel the Elder, the still life was acquired by the Oslo museum as a prized possession in 1845. According to curator Cynthia Osiecki, the painting was shipped off to storage after experts retracted the Brueghel attribution in the early 20th century.

item.title: The Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalists Highlight the Sorrowful and Sublime - Colossal
item.description:
Our oceans are places of mystery and biological wonders as much as they are essential to communities’ livelihoods. We tap these expansive bodies of water for recreation, food, transportation. From the Atlantic to the Arctic, oceans cover around 70 percent of the earth’s surface, and there is an incredible wealth of life yet to be discovered.

As the continuing climate crisis melts ice caps and raises sea levels, and industrial fishing and waste threatens endangered marine animals and habitats, reminders of the oceans’ irreplaceable value and power are ever more critical. That’s where Oceanographic magazine and Blancpain’s annual Ocean Photographer of the Year contest comes in as a catalyst for conservation.

This year’s finalists span categories from Adventure and Human Connection to Ocean Unseen and Conservation. To really delve into the complexity of issues facing our saltwater expanses, the latter is organized in two parts: Hope and Impact. Throughout, there is a sense that in order for people to really become aware of the problems facing our oceans, let alone feel motivated to act, we need to understand both the beauty and the terribleness of these waters, whether inherent or human-inflicted.

Founder and director Will Harrison describes the contest as a platform for stories to reach the world. “These photographs don’t just capture what’s beneath the surface; they surface the stories our planet most needs us to hear. As the pressures on our ocean grow, so does the importance of the artists who bear witness to them.”

The winners will be announced in September. See all the finalists in the competition’s online gallery, and follow updates on Instagram.

item.title: Nathaniel Mary Quinn’s Fragments of Home - Hyperallergic
item.description:
CHICAGO — More than 10 million people in the United States have called public housing home over the past century, yet the country boasts only one museum dedicated to the subject. The National Public Housing Museum (NPHM), after nearly two decades as a roving entity, opened a permanent home in Chicago in early 2025. It seeks to address one of the most intersectional of histories, connecting art, design, architecture, human rights, politics, social policy, the economy, systemic racism, immigration trends, policing practices, and more.

The museum occupies the sole remaining section of the Jane Addams Homes, constructed in 1938 on the southwest side of Chicago. It’s currently surrounded by an empty lot nearly the size of a city block, courtesy the Chicago Housing Authority’s Plan of Transformation, launched back in 1999 to solve the problem of deteriorating buildings, unsafe projects, and racial segregation with widescale demolition and the mostly unfulfilled promise of replacement mixed-income housing for all. That plan eventually amounted to the largest net loss of affordable housing in the country’s history. This story is just one of many told at the NPHM via an engaging combination of archival, experiential, historic, and artistic displays.

The day I visited, offerings included an exhibit devoted to personal objects lent by public housing residents across the country, from a hand-stitched wedding dress and a heavyweight championship belt to an item I found especially relatable, a rotary phone with an extra-long cord. A case study of a rare recent success story, the Millers River Apartments in Cambridge, Massachusetts, nearly broke my head with its meticulous dissection of the impossibly complicated American tax credit system. Especially generous are a pair of apartment units recreating the homes of specific families representative of particular eras: the Turovitzes, Jewish immigrants who were among the first to occupy the Jane Addams Homes, and the Hatches, an African-American couple with eight children who moved in in 1960. A third apartment, set in the 1950s, screens an immersive film explaining what happened in between from a policy perspective, including redlining and racist covenants, via the entrancing silhouette puppetry of the performance collective Manual Cinema.

The museum’s courtyard delights with large limestone animal sculptures, designed by local polymath Edgar Miller for the Jane Addams Homes’ original outdoor play area, now beautifully restored. Also outside are three bang-up works of public art. “Still Here: Zhegagoynak,” a palimpsestic 40-foot-tall (~12.2m) mural by Andrea Carlson, acknowledges the land under the NPHM as being unceded by the Potawatomi. Amanda Williams and Olalekan Jeyifous fashioned an exuberant glass entry portico splashed with colors taken from paint chips left behind when the building’s final residents were forced to move out — vivid hues applied to apartment walls in defiance of Chicago Housing Authority rules mandating beige or light green. Over in the parking lot, Marisa Morán Jahn and Rafi Segal invented new ways to play basketball using a tricycle-mounted hoop system and a radically reimagined court design.

That the NPHM excels in bringing together advanced art and social history comes as no surprise given the credentials of its executive director, Lisa Yun Lee, who has helmed some of Chicago’s most important socially engaged art institutions, from the Hull-House Museum to Open Engagement to the UIC School of Art & Art History. Under her curation, this summer, the NPHM opened Nathaniel Mary Quinn: A Love Letter to My Mother, its first temporary exhibition dedicated to a single artist, also Quinn’s first solo institutional showing in his hometown. Represented by mega-gallery Gagosian and recently in the news for having illustrated the Rolling Stones’ latest album, Quinn grew up in the Robert Taylor Homes on Chicago’s South Side, a place he described as being “incredibly efficient at killing dreams.” His show includes a reading room detailing how the project, the largest in the city and at one point the world, went from Mayor Daley’s proud ribbon-cutting in 1962 to decades of systemic neglect, eroding services, and eventual demolition.

A Love Letter to My Mother is a spare show. Ten portraits on canvas and paper surround a living room meant to evoke Quinn’s family home circa 1984. It was the artist’s first studio, where he sketched directly on the walls; when he ran out of space, his mother washed the old drawings away so he could start anew. At NPHM, each artwork incarnates a person Quinn knew either during his early life or after he moved to Brooklyn as an adult. Extended captions include intimate recollections of his father, a family friend named Junebug, and two flashy guys from his block in Crown Heights. Every one of Quinn’s likenesses is lifelike and demanding of attention, but no one is easy to look at. Fragments of a young neighbor named Erika, her wide dark nose and full lips tenderly rendered, slice sharply into the pale forehead and velvety shoulder of a reproduction of Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” (1665). Each segment radiates beauty, but their collision partly blinds the girl, and the proportions fit grotesquely. “Charles: Re-visited," a large bust of the artist’s estranged brother, awkwardly pieces together the fragile mouth and ear of a little boy, the sharp eyes and fedora of a swaggering man, the nose of a bull, a sleeve of streetwear, and an unexpectedly feminine scarf, all in contradictory stylistic registers. The effect unsettles, one aspect obliterating another, the person violently incoherent.

Quinn presents each of his subjects likewise, channeling the critical media mashup of Hannah Höch, the psychological miasma of Francis Bacon, and the rhythmic vitality of Romare Bearden. Arranged from shards, in mismatched angles and aesthetics, their visages look at once battered and lovely, festive and bleak, a human emerging but only just. They hold together via a signature “paint-drawing” technique Quinn has been refining since 2013, resulting in composite portraits that look like collage, down to the edges of white left between what appear to be slices of 17th-century Dutch paintings intercut with slivers of Avedon photographs and bits of anonymous news footage and glossy magazine ads. But, crucially, are not collage, having been crafted seamlessly from a combination of oil paint, charcoal, gouache, paint stick, and pastel. Collage, made of stuck-together scraps originating somewhere else, communicates temporariness, incompleteness, dependence. Quinn’s people comprise multiple parts, under extreme duress, but that is their perennial state. They are not there to be rearranged. 

The Robert Taylor Homes were demolished about two decades ago, long after Quinn left to attend an elite military academy in Indiana on full scholarship. His mother, Mary, died soon after. His family dispersed; he has remained estranged from them ever since. Before graduating, Quinn added Mary’s name to his own so that she, who never finished high school, would also be recognized on his diploma, as she has been on every diploma, honor, collection placard, museum label, gallery announcement, and magazine article — including this one — ever since. It’s a situation of consequent political and philosophical reordering — requiring consideration of a person otherwise relegated to the margins of public life — akin to the realignment aesthetically achieved by Quinn’s portraiture, from which it is equally impossible to turn away.

Nathaniel Mary Quinn: A Love Letter to My Mother continues at the National Public Housing Museum (919 South Ada Street, Chicago, Illinois) through August 23. The exhibition was curated by Lisa Yun Lee.

item.title: Divers Stumble Upon 2,000-Year-Old Roman Shipwreck in Italy - Hyperallergic
item.description:
While exploring the warm waters of the Sicilian coast last week, two Italian divers discovered hundreds of clay vessels piled atop an approximately 2,000-year-old Roman shipwreck.

In an Instagram post chronicling the discovery, Giacomo De Mola recalled finding the site with his diving partner, Igor Bisulli, after mistaking the wreck for a "big rock."

Sicilian cultural authorities clarified in a statement that the ship resides at a depth of 46 meters (151 feet) and primarily carries Dressel 1A amphorae (named after the German archaeologist Heinrich Dressel), late Roman Republic ceramic wine jars characterized by their angularity, pointed base, and collared rim. The divers also unearthed two anchor stumps and an unidentifiable lead structure.

"The discovery is, to me, now very exciting," De Mola told Hyperallergic. "I did not expect it to be so important."

Italian Minister of Culture Alessandro Giuli described the site in a statement to Hyperallergic as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years."

Underwater photos of the discovery, which De Mola shared with Hyperallergic, show piles of amphorae overgrown with sea life. In each image, the signature vessel shape remains prominent, with glimpses of the original red clay base peeking through thick crusts of barnacles and vegetation. Dated between the second and first centuries BCE, the wreck could provide further insights into Ancient Rome's war-torn expansion throughout the Mediterranean.

De Mola speculated that the wreck could also contain Lamboglia 2 amphorae, along with clay jars from Neo-Punic-era North Africa. Sicilian authorities have not yet disclosed the classifications of the amphorae and their contents.

The discovery recalls other ancient Roman shipwreck findings in recent years. In 2019, over 300 amphorae were found in the hull of a 1,700-year-old vessel in Mallorca. Two years later, another collection of amphorae was discovered off the coast of Palermo.

"The sea never ceases to amaze us," De Mola wrote on Instagram. "This time we didn’t find just a wreck. We found a piece of our history."

item.title: RIP Vermeer, You Would’ve Hated AI - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Every book is a record of the life of the people who thumbed through it, the binder who secured its pages in place, the designers who chose its cover and typeset. So, when news emerged that Anthropic scanned and destroyed out-of-print titles to train Claude, it felt like a gut-punch to the very spirit of storytelling and artmaking that has always sustained our humanity.

This week, author Ed Simon articulates the fascist logic behind this destruction, and reminds us why we must keep reading, writing, and critiquing in the face of it. Writer Natasha Seaman, for one, had mixed feelings about a new book on Vermeer, who has amassed a devoted following in part because his personal history still largely remains a mystery. Read her sharp review of the biography below, plus the latest in art book news.

As for me, I’m counteracting the technocracy’s affront on books by revisiting old favorites (Pride & Prejudice, yes, I am an Austenphile) and discovering new ones (Valeria Luiselli’s Beginning Middle End and Jennifer Higgie’s Bedlam). Put that in your algo and smoke it, Anthropic.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

AI Companies Are Pulping Our Humanity

After Spanish physician and theologian Michael Servetus was burnt at the stake in 1553 for religious heresy, only three surviving copies of his The Restoration of Christianity would be spared from the bonfire. One particular copy, now held by the University of Edinburgh library, is ironically believed to have been personally saved by the Protestant leader John Calvin, who was responsible for Servetus’s execution in Geneva. Anyone familiar with Calvin, who bragged in a letter that he had “purged the Church of so pernicious a monster,” knows that the book wasn’t preserved due to affection for Servetus, but rather a bibliophile’s sentiment — even a doctrinaire, zealous, tyrannical bibliophile.

And yet, as bizarre as Calvin’s motivations might have been, he’s still not as noxious as the artificial intelligence companies, including Anthropic, that have been involved in bulk purchasing, digitizing, and then pulping out-of-print books to train their large language models. Calvin at least had the excuse of his God; AI companies don’t even have that. | Ed Simon

item.title: Divers Discover Hundreds of Ancient Ceramic Vessels Amid Shipwreck Off the Coast of Sicily - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Divers with a specialized unit of the Carabinieri, Italy’s military police, have uncovered a 2,000-year-old shipwreck on the ocean floor off the northwest coast of Sicily. In a Facebook post on August 7, Alessandro Giuli, Italy’s culture minister, said that this is “one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries in recent years.”

According to the BBC, local fishermen alerted the Carabinieri to the shipwreck, which was full of hundreds of ancient Roman vessels called amphorae. The boat itself is nearly 70 feet long and 20 feet wide, and was discovered at a depth of 150 feet.

Italian spearfisherman and freediver Giacomo De Mola posted a video on Instagram on August 8 describing “without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life.” De Mola recounts that he and a friend, Igor Bisulli, were scanning the seabed off the coast of Mazara del Vallo with their StructureScan, which uses sonar technology to view underwater terrain in 3D. What he thought was a large rock turned out to be an ancient ship full of hundreds of pieces of well-preserved pottery. There are also two anchors and a lead pipe. “It is hard to describe the feeling of being among the first humans in nearly twenty centuries to see that place again,” De Mora wrote.

 In a statement, the Carabinieri designated the location of the shipwreck as a “significant underwater archaeological site” and explained that the site will undergo detailed documentation and study overseen by the Superintendency of the Sea.

item.title: National Gallery of Art Protects Works Ahead of Trump's IndyCar Race - Hyperallergic
item.description:
An IndyCar race taking place in the nation’s capital later this month as part of President Trump's “Freedom 250” celebrations is under scrutiny as experts study the possible impact of race car vibrations on thousands of artworks held in museum collections near the track.

The National Gallery of Art (NGA), one of several institutions located on the 1.7-mile Freedom 250 Grand Prix circuit — along with the Hirshhorn Museum, the National Archives, and the National Museum of the American Indian, and others — conducted a study to examine possible consequences “out of a great abundance of caution,” a spokesperson said.

“Based on the results, we have implemented a set of measures to ensure the safety of our staff, visitors, collection, and facilities during the race,” the NGA spokesperson told Hyperallergic in a statement, noting that the museum is not disclosing specific findings.

According to the New Republic, some artworks at the Washington, DC, museum have been reinstalled to face away from the side of the building that faces the racetrack. Further images from the Washington Post showed that some outdoor artworks had been boarded up, including I.M. Pei's skylights in front of the museum's East building.

A White House spokesperson told Hyperallergic that the White House and IndyCar's parent company, Penske Corporation, "have followed all appropriate protocols and been in close coordination with all relevant agencies to ensure this is also the safest and most secure race for all visitors to enjoy.” (Penske Corporation is owned by Republican donor Roger Penske, who is the father of Jay Penske, founder of Penske Media Corporation.)

item.title: Ireland’s Museum Staffers Struggle with Precarious Contracts and Toxic Environments - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Museum staffers in Ireland are finding it increasingly difficult to sustain a career in the field over unstable contracts, low pay and toxic working environments, according to Dr. Emma McAlister, who wrote a blog post on the issue for the International Council of Museums on Monday.

As McAlister recounted, she has only been able to work in the Irish museum industry over the last two and a half years through a temporary rolling contract that, at times, would be renewed just one day before its expiration. Her experience isn’t isolated.

A 2024 compensation study from the lobby group Irish Museums Association found there was an overreliance on temporary contracts and volunteers in the country’s museums. Around 52 percent of museum workers were on permanent or rolling contracts with volunteers making up their second largest pool, standing at 27 percent, IMA said in the report. Only 6 percent of workers were on fixed-term contracts for up to five years. The transition from short-term contracts to permanent positions is a fundamental issue Ireland’s museums need to address, the IMA concluded in its report.

Temporary contracts add to instability, McAlister wrote, and create a culture of silence around employee mistreatment and toxic hierarchies. Ireland’s museums in particular have a reputation for unhealthy working cultures, she wrote. For instance, one in five workers were “often” bullied at the National Museum of Ireland, according to a previous Irish Times report.

Due to the prestigious nature of these cultural institutions, there’s an “expectation of gratitude” despite low pay and toxic hierarchies. This is not just limited to museums in Ireland. In the UK, 16 percent of staffers working in cultural activities were paid below living wage in 2024, according to the Museums Association, a UK-based membership organization for museum, gallery and heritage professionals and organizations.

One underlying issue that results in museum staffers being underpaid with fragile job security lies in the underfunding of the museum sector. But some governments have pledged recent investments into established and local museums as a means to boost the sector.

On Friday, Ireland’s Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport, Patrick O’Donovan earmarked €274,000 ($316,000) for local and regional museums in the country. Meanwhile, Northern Ireland’s Ulster Folk Museum also received £40 million ($54 million) in government funding.

Ireland’s funding boost follows the UK’s £1.5 billion pledge over a five-year time period, £600 million of which will be pledged to Department-funded museums, such as the British Museum and the National Portrait Gallery, while £160 million has been pledged for regional and local institutions.

While further government funding is a positive signal the museum sector could be moving in the right direction, it isn’t yet clear how the new budgets will be used by individual museums, and if some of the new funds will be directed toward staff retention.

Fundamentally, the Irish museum sector needs to “face a long-overdue reckoning” with help from governments and funding bodies, McAlister said.

item.title: How Betye Saar Came to Be - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — There is an African Adinkra symbol, “Sankofa,” that means “go back and get it.” It’s intended to preach the importance of looking to the past when shaping the future, and to share wisdom between generations. On the occasion of her 100th birthday, Roberts Projects in Los Angeles organized an exhibition to recognize the earliest professional works of Betye Saar — the prolific assemblage artist who prodded the psyche of the Black American experience for over seven decades before her death last month. The show sheds light on a lesser-known facet of her canon: costume design. 

Through the over 200 archival objects in the show, one gets a good sense of the multiple pots Saar had her fingers in at the beginning of her career. Costume design, dancing (a full-wall photo of a young dancing Saar acts as the exhibition greeter), photography, drawing, jewelry, garments, greeting cards, album covers, and more are on view. The range depicts Saar’s broad curiosities, but it also underlines her particular skill in identifying various potentials and fitting them together. 

Some of the first archival photographs in the show are costume and set designs for a 1970 production of Antigone at the Inner City Cultural Center (ICCC), then located at the intersection of Washington and Vermont in Los Angeles. Saar worked on the costumes for the play but also did the backgrounds; the wallpaper was her first foray into collage work. “I just love materials,” Saar said during a press walkthrough of the show. “This was one of the first times I really got to play with that sort of collage work long before I knew what assemblage was.” 

In fact, this entire exhibition is an ode to Saar discovering the practice of mixing media for which she would become internationally recognized. In her costume work, she reimagined second-hand clothes into abstract garments for the stage or gathered found materials to fashion into accessories. Her sketches and fabric swatches are displayed in vitrines underneath photos of the designs in situ. With certain productions, she explained during the walkthrough, she would “often break down some of the stage work to a smaller scale to sell in the gift shop.” That idea is reminiscent of her classic assemblage work “Black Girl’s Window” (1969), made around the same era. In addition to the early costumes, the exhibition highlights Saar’s domestic creations for her three daughters — Lezley, Alison, and Tracye (plus Tracye’s stuffed bear “Tutti”) — and homemade outfits for the very first years of the Renaissance Pleasure Faire.

item.title: Looted Ivorian “Talking Drum” Arrives at Its Home Village After More Than a Century - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A sacred “talking drum” known as the Djidji Ayôkwé, looted from Côte d’Ivoire by French colonial troops over a century ago, returned this month to the place where it was made. According to the Namibia Press Agency (NAMPA), the drum arrived on August 7 at its home village of Adjame, where the local community was able to see it for the first time.

The ten-foot-long, 940-pound drum has a single-piece cylindrical soundbox slit in half longitudinally. Extending out from the slit are two planks, one of which supports a carving of a jumping leopard. The box itself is decorated with carved and painted faces and geometric patterns.

The massive instrument was once used by Côte d’Ivoire’s Atchan/Ebrié people to transmit messages between villages many miles apart, including warnings of impending French recruitment operations. It was seized by colonial authorities in 1916 as a way of suppressing local resistance.

Between 1916 and 1930, the Djidji Ayôkwé was kept outside the French governor’s Ivorian home. It was transferred to France in 1929 and housed most recently at Paris’s Musée Quai Branly, where it recently underwent restoration.

The drum topped a list of 148 objects that Côte d’Ivoire requested from France in 2019; the petition followed French President Emmanuel Macron’s 2017 pledge to return works of art looted in Africa during the colonial era.

Following a 2025 vote by the French parliament to authorize its repatriation, the Djidji Ayôkwé was handed over to the Republic of Côte d’Ivoire in a ceremony at the Musée Quai Branly in February. It arrived in Côte d’Ivoire in March but had not been taken out of its crate until now.

Ensconced in a glass case mounted on a float, the drum was paraded through the Yopougon district of Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire’s largest city, before continuing on to Adjame. There it was met by Ivorian minister of culture Francoise Remarck, along with local dignitaries and residents.

“A nation cannot develop if it doesn’t preserve its memory and promote its heritage,” Adjame mayor Farikou Soumahoro said.

“We want to see the drum with our own eyes so we can truly believe it belongs to us,” said villager Jacqueline Akrebie.

Traditional leader Cyriaque Ahoure said he had come to share a moment of “great joy, when we remember our ancestors.”

The drum will be exhibited at the Museum of Civilizations in Abidjan.

In recent years, institutions and collectors in the U.S. and Europe have faced increasing pressure to return cultural property to its original communities. In April, France passed a new law facilitating the restitution of items illegally acquired between 1815 and 1972.

item.title: Family Memories and Midwestern Niceties Converge in Melissa Joseph’s ‘Casserole Culture’ - Colossal
item.description:
Unlike the coasts, Midwestern culture is synonymous with the manual labor of blue-collar jobs, resilience necessary in harsh winters, and a certain friendliness that lends itself to a deep-rooted sense of community. These humble tenets grounded Melissa Joseph’s childhood in Saint Marys, a small, rural city in Pennsylvania, where she was born to a mother with Irish heritage and a father from Kerala, India. The melange of biracial life, Midwestern niceties, and gendered fiber art traditions are woven through Joseph’s artistic practice, which translates family photos into tender needle-felted scenes.

In her forthcoming solo exhibition, Casserole Culture, the New York-based artist echoes the warmth and mundanity present in these snapshots of life through soft layers of wool. An upturned hat on a wooden dresser, the bright orange flowers of dining room wallpaper, and even the titular hot dish all appear in hazy fiber, nodding to the fuzziness of memory.

Alongside two-dimensional works, Joseph also incorporates found objects like worn tires, salvaged boxes, frames, and industrial materials into her more sculptural pieces. In this body of work, a felted fire roars inside a hulking model hearth, for example, while another embeds a fragment of a fork inside a metal-and-wood form.

The artist’s mother died in 2024, and she’s found it difficult to depict her family in the wake of such profound grief, instead focusing on their possessions and the places where cherished moments occurred. “Even if the people themselves may elude the artist’s hand, she captures the spaces they enliven, the unremarkable yet prized moments that shape our lives,” says a statement about the exhibition.

Casserole Culture will be on view from September 9 to October 17 at Charles Moffett in New York. Until then, explore more of Joseph’s work on Instagram.

item.title: Three Public Artworks by Banksy Have Cost UK Taxpayers Almost $200,000 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Banksy’s guerrilla artworks have generated millions of dollars in auction sales and drawn crowds wherever they appear. They’ve also left British taxpayers footing a growing cleanup bill.

Public authorities across London have spent nearly $203,000 removing, protecting, and managing three of the anonymous street artist’s works since 2024, according to figures obtained by the BBC through Freedom of Information requests. The total will keep going up as officials continue efforts to erase one of the artist’s latest murals from the walls of London’s Royal Courts of Justice last year.

The work, depicting a judge in a wig striking a protester with a gavel, has cost Britain’s Ministry of Justice $67,000 in removal efforts so far, with another $48,000 spent on security and staff overtime while the work stayed up. Contractors now are using laser technology after initial cleaning attempts failed, and officials have said that replacing the affected stonework might be the next step if those efforts are unsuccessful. 

The mural has reignited a familiar debate over whether Banksy’s modus operandi should be treated as criminal vandalism or culturally significant public art. Critics, including Britain’s Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy, argued taxpayers should not bear the cost of cleaning what he described as damage to a national symbol of the rule of law. Others defended the work, saying Banksy’s murals attract visitors and make art accessible outside traditional museums and galleries. 

The court mural is only the latest example.

In April, Westminster City Council said it spent nearly $81,000 on safety barriers, security, and administrative costs after Banksy secretly installed a statue in Waterloo Place near Trafalgar Square. The council, which became the legal owner of the sculpture because it sits on public land, said it is still considering what to do with the work. 

Earlier, in August 2024, the City of London removed a police sentry box that Banksy had transformed with painted piranha fish at a cost of almost $3,000. Rather than being relegated to the scrap yard, the structure was placed into storage and is scheduled to go on public display when the London Museum reopens in November.

item.title: Fossils and Other Exhibits Stolen From German University in Latest Museum Robbery - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The University of Bonn in Germany announced last week that numerous fossils and other exhibits have been stolen from its Goldfuß Museum. The university is now appealing to the public for information on items put up for sale or found on display, in order to secure their recovery.

The university said it is not clear when the items were stolen, but that it occured during renovation work, which began in December 2023 and is ongoing. In a blog post published August 7, the university shared images of the missing items, and asked the public for assistance.

“Anyone who has spotted one of the items shown, seen them being offered for sale—e.g. online, on fossil shows, trading platforms or in a store—or noticed anything else that might be relevant is asked to contact the Bonn Police without delay,” the blog post reads, directing the public to send tips to Bonn Police’s Criminal Investigation Division.

The university “strongly advise[d]” people not to contact the sellers on their own, but to pass along detais.

“Besides the damage caused to the museum building and the theoretical market value of individual items, however, the theft also represents a loss of considerable intellectual significance, as every exhibit stolen from the historical collection, which stretches back to the institute’s founder Georg August Goldfuß (1782—1848), can now no longer be used for research or teaching purposes,” the blog post continues.

Per a separate FAQ, the university said that the theft was discovered after certain wooden safety enclosures were due to be dismantled. Workers found the cases broken into and the items, detailed in photos, missing.

The incident is just the latest theft at a major museum in Europe. While last October’s brazen daylight Louvre robbery has captured headlines and public attention, there have numerous robberies since, including an all-night robbery in Italy in late July in which thieves made off with $4.63 million worth of art.

item.title: Inhotim Founder Bernardo Paz to Open a Namesake Museum, Right Next Door - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Brazil’s Minas Gerais will soon see another museum thanks to mining magnate Bernardo Paz, the megacollector behind the Inhotim museum and nature complex. The Museu Bernardo Paz will turn 311 acres of countryside into a new landscape for “art, nature and community.” The first phase will open in September 2027. 

“Museu Bernardo Paz is taking root and flourishing from a belief in the creative potential of unexpected encounters,” said Paz in press materials. “This is a place to discover new relationships between art and landscapes of different kinds, between artists and audiences that have not yet met one another, and between the community of Brumadinho and visitors from all over the world. All of this is coming together here, and all of it is for the people.”

The museum will encompass more than 20 galleries and pavilions, with commissioned outdoor installations and sculptures, all set in a landscape that includes a lush botanical park and a forest. Locals will be able to take advantage of a community center with a library and art studios. One of the pavilions in development will be devoted to music and dancing, “essential elements of Brazilian culture and identity,” according to the organizers.

The first phase will include pavilions dedicated to the work of Laura Belém, Sandra Gamarra, Sonia Gomes, Michael Heizer, Anna Maria Maiolino, and Pedro Moraleida, as well as major large-scale sculptures and environments by Torkwase Dyson, Frida Orupabo, Giuseppe Penone, and Mario Garcia Torres. Heizer’s pavilion, the first permanent installation in Latin America, is in progress, and will be dedicated to two large-scale 1993 installations, Displaced Replaced Mass #3 and Negative Wall Sculpture #1.

“At a moment when there is a prevailing global sense of ever-narrowing possibilities—whether in culture, society, the environment, or politics—we hope that Museu Bernardo Paz will be a place that renews the imagination,” said Paulo Miyada, artistic director, in the press release. “In a landscape full of conjunctions that challenge established notions of museum and landscape, intense opportunities emerge for creation, inspiration, and transformation.”

Paz, who has frequently ranked on the ARTnews Top 200 Collectors list, co-founded Inhotim in 2006 with New York art advisor Allan Schwartzman, who is also chief curatorial advisor on the new museum. Residing on a 700-acre campus, the museum mixed art, some of it new commissions, with nature preserves and imported flora. It features major pieces by a who’s-who of contemporary art, including international figures such as Doug Aitken, Matthew Barney, Chris Burden, Yayoi Kusama and David Lamelas, as well as Brazilian artists including Cildo Meireles, Hélio Oiticica, Lygia Pape, Valeska Soares, and Adriana Varejão.

The new museum complex in the Brumadinho region will also feature some 15,000 trees and a million shrubs, cacti, and flowering plants in a design inspired by Paz’s relationship with 20th-century landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx. Striking arrangements of fruit trees and flowering trees are promised for a space that borders the Inhotim Private Natural Heritage Reserve and the Paz Environmental Protection Area. 

“Bernardo Paz opened up unprecedented possibilities for contemporary art museums when he founded Inhotim 20 years ago,” said Schwartzman. “With that landmark institution now established, he is moving beyond it into new experimental territory. There is a creative abundance at Museu Bernardo Paz—a distinctive and radical sense of discovery—that will be astonishing in both scope and imaginative force.”

In 2017, Paz was sentenced to nine years in jail for money laundering related to Inhotim, but the decision was reversed in 2020.

item.title: ‘Remember Me’ Highlights Black Americans’ Self-Expression in Early Photography - Colossal
item.description:
In our era of screens and proliferous imagery, it strains the imagination to comprehend a time before photography. Two centuries ago, an inventor named Nicéphore Niépce took the very first picture of his courtyard in France by fitting a pewter plate into a camera obscura. A few years later, a professional scene painter named Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre conceived of the aptly named daguerreotype, in which the image could be permanently fixed. He and Niépce both sold their technologies to the French government, which then published a how-to guide and facilitated the global spread of the process. In 1939, the first daguerrotypes were created in the U.S.

As they say, the rest is history. Except, we often only see a part of the whole story. Because the technology was expensive, and therefore having your photograph taken (let alone owning the equipment) was costly, the visual record of the 19th century in this medium is heavily skewed toward affluent, white individuals and families who could afford it. Due to the long exposure time required to capture the images, we also don’t see candid shots, as carefully posed scenes were required for clarity and fidelity.

Photography was invented decades before the Civil War and the end of slavery in the U.S., yet so rarely do we glimpse real faces that “illuminate the complexities of race, freedom, and agency before, during, and after the Civil War,” says the National Gallery of Art, which presents Remember Me: Picturing African Americans in Early Photography later this year. The exhibition brings forward dozens of images taken of and by Black Americans, showcasing a wide variety of lived experiences in one place.

Fashion, family, and social status are on full display in a range of gelatin silver prints, daguerrotypes, tintypes, and ambrotypes, some of which are colorized. Because many of the earliest formats were very fragile, they were often displayed in ornate folding cases. Several of these will be included with their images, plus cabinet cards and portraits by pioneering Black artists like James Van Der Zee, who ran a prominent studio in Harlem in the early 20th century.

The exhibition will highlight around 70 pieces in the museum’s collection that center self-expression and the entrepreneurial spirit of African American individuals. Remember Me is slated to open on November 7 and will continue through March 14 in Washington, D.C. Learn more and plan your visit on the museum’s website.

item.title: The Native History of NYC's Oysters - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The oyster, writes Hrag Vartanian, is "no incidental New Yorker, but perhaps its most symbolic creature." Hyperallergic's co-founder and editor-at-large visits Mohawk artist Alan Michelson’s poetic installation in Governor’s Island, where about a million oyster shells culled from Manhattan restaurants stir reflections on Native land and historical memory.
