item.title: Joeun Kim Aatchim’s Layered Lines Summon Translucent Worlds - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In Joeun Kim Aatchim’s paintings—but she calls them drawings—everything is so vivid, yet so elusive. Her line feels definitive, yet the images they convey seem to fade away into sheer luminosity. 

Her works are typically painted using mineral pigment in shellac—sometimes with watercolor, pastel, or other materials—on layers of silk that, stretched across frames, show through to the wall behind. They’re all about one image being seen through another—not different things, in the manner of Francis Picabia’s transparencies, but different versions of the same thing; different attempts, a little like the way Henri Matisse would partially overpaint his works to show multiple thoughts about how to depict one thing, or how to position it within the composition. 

Aatchim speaks about her method as being a layering of first drafts. “Rather than working on a piece over and over to make it perfect,” she told me, “I can keep my first thought” even as the piece develops. The result is a bouquet of essays, finding resolution in the tentative. She calls what she does “drawing” because she considers it “a thought in progress,” and because her materials never completely cover the surface she’s working on. “It doesn’t matter if it’s pencil or chalk or paint. If it doesn’t cover the surface, I consider that a drawing, whether it’s on the floor, on the street, or on the wall, or an object.”

The Korean-born artist has been exhibiting widely since earning her MFA at Columbia University in 2017, where she’d gone at the suggestion of Kiki Smith, to whom she’d been an assistant. Since then, she’s had solo shows at galleries in New York, Los Angeles, Guadalajara, Seoul, and Madrid. Coming later this year is her first exhibition in São Paulo, at Almeida & Dale. I caught up with Aatchim not in her Brooklyn studio but in Seoul, by Zoom, while she was visiting her parents. Was she working there? “I tried to rest, but I don’t know how to rest, and I don’t have any hobbies,” she said. “I started thinking, maybe I’m nobody if I’m not making art. So I started making work in the dining room.” In any case, she added, the materials she likes to use are more readily available in Korea than in New York.

But maybe, her real material is mnemonic. She considers her vivid sense of recall to be both a blessing and a curse. She explains that “memories I haven’t drawn yet keep lingering in my head, and have to be stored somewhere. You know, because I stored this somewhere safe, I can now get new memories.” That probably explains why her simple yet multilayered portraits of friends and observations of her everyday world can be at once so clear and distinct yet so intangible. After all, memories can’t be fixed. They’re always thoughts in progress.

item.title: New York Socialite Tracey Amon Asks Court to Compel Advisor Sandy Heller to Turn Over Papers Connected to Late Ex-Husband’s Art Collection - ARTnews.com
item.description:
New York’s Tracey Amon filed a request on July 25 in the US District Court for the District of Southern New York to subpoena art advisor Sanford “Sandy” Heller. She wants him to turn over documents for use in her lawsuits in Switzerland over the disposition of the assets of her late husband, Maurice Alain Amon, who retained Heller as an advisor starting in 2013. Heller has been described as “possibly the biggest art advisor in the world,” and reputedly works with Roman Abramovich and Steve Cohen.

The heir to the company SIPCA, which makes inks used in printing currency, Maurice died at 68 in 2019 while on holiday in Saint Tropez. The filing puts his value at some $600 million in assets and business interests at the time of his death, and asserts that Tracey is looking for her rightful share. The request revolves around Heller’s valuation of the collection.

The two married in Hong Kong in 2008 “without signing a marriage contract on that occasion or later,” according to an exhibit. He filed abroad for divorce in 2015 without telling her, says the filing, which claims he secretly removed some 20 artworks, collectively valued at $25 million, from their New York home. He allegedly also spirited away artworks from other residences. He claimed in court filings in 2017 that after losing her key, she took a blowtorch to a lockbox in their Paris home, allegedly leaving a toxic dust over artworks by the likes of Jean-Michel Basquiat, Damien Hirst, Richard Prince, Gerhard Richter, Cy Twombly and Andy Warhol.

While the divorce was in process, he allegedly executed a will naming Albert Amon, his son from a previous marriage, as his only heir, and his assistant, Silvio Venturi, as executor. The New York Post reported that in 2018, she had won about $123,000 a month in spousal support and a lump sum of about $1.3 million in a Monaco court. He allegedly added other legatees and beneficiaries in a codicil executed in Singapore in 2019. She sued Albert and Venturi in Switzerland in 2020; they also brought an action against her.

The Justice of the Peace in Lausanne ordered the administration of the estate in December 2024. Administrator Olivier Weniger issued an inventory in December 2025, along with a report from accounting firm KPMG with an evaluation of the art holdings as of 2019 of Artmon, the holding company through which Amon held his artworks, which was registered in the British Virgin Islands. 

“It appears that the value of Artmon’s artworks diminished dramatically during 2019,” says the filing, adding, “This diminution appears to be based at least partially on Heller’s valuation.” Heller reported capital losses of €33.4 million and latent capital gains of €7.5 million, for a loss of about €26 million, or $29.6 million. “But,” says the filing (in bold type and italics), “there is no list of the works Heller actually examined, no methodology provided, and no information as to when Heller did its evaluation.”

Heller did not immediately return a request for comment.

Tracey Amon is seeking the complete valuation report and all associated work product, including the list of artworks examined, comparables considered, the valuation methodology, and all relevant correspondence. She also seeks documentation of all of Heller’s dealings with Artmon and the Maurice Amon estate, including any art sales, art purchases, consignments, inventories, invoices, and the like.

The court has yet to respond to Amon’s request.

item.title: The Lost Pearls of New York City - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Walking down Pearl Street in lower Manhattan, you probably don’t realize that the name marks the original 17th-century East River shoreline of New York City. In fact, the street was named for a Lenape shell midden that was located on its southern section, which is also believed to have been adjacent to a Lenape canoe landing. It was one of many prominent middens that marked the region, and as Mark Kurlansky explains in his bestselling book The Big Oyster: History on the Half Shell (2006), middens are “the most common marker of a pre-European settlement anywhere in the area of the mouth of the Hudson.” These piles of oyster shells, he notes, were sometimes as much as four feet deep, sometimes buried in the ground, sometimes piled high.

The early 17th-century Dutch colonists were the first to note these large piles and many of them remained well into the 19th century when the last vestiges were dismantled and then used as filler for roads and other modernization projects. Brooklyn writer Daniel Tredwell wrote in his 1839 diary that he would explore these piles with his father:

 “On the way out we pass many Indian shell heaps bleached as white as snow, which they much resemble at a distance. Some of them on the banks of the creek extend from fifteen to thirty feet upon the bank, and under water, in many instances entirely across the creek. These shell heaps, long ere this, has excited our curiosity and we had proposed all manner of questioning concerning their authors. These questions my father did not and could not satisfactorily answer, and we were consequently unsatisfied, and hence there was a constantly recurring inquiry.”

The passage highlights that the erasure of Indigenous settlement was so thorough in 19th-century New York that it never occurred to the Tredwell family that the landmarks they visited were consciously created by those whom they displaced. 

That forgetting is at the foundation of Alan Michelson’s “The Oyster” project, which opened this past weekend on Governors Island and will continue until late fall. This history, Michelson’s public artwork suggests, is still present, and equally contested, as people who live here continue to ignore the mark that the oyster has on our daily lives.

item.description:
In 1961, Yoko Ono dedicated one of her famous screaming pieces to performance artist Simone Forti, who died in Los Angeles last week. That same year, Forti debuted her piece Five Dance Constructions and Some Other Things in Ono’s Manhattan loft. Simone Forti Talks Yoko Ono, Dance, and Aging in Never-Before-Published Interview

About a dozen years ago, I happened to be simultaneously writing two different essays about two of the most influential artists of the 20th century who are almost exact contemporaries: Simone Forti (born in Italy in 1935) and Yoko Ono (born in Japan in 1933). Only two years apart, these women had many other things in common besides age: They were both transcultural migrants whose early lives were shaped by the deprivations of fascism and war. Both experienced discrimination — Forti’s Jewish family left Italy as a result of Mussolini’s Racial Laws, while Ono was (and still is) by turns exoticized and vilified as an Asian woman.

As cross-disciplinary groundbreakers, both Forti and Ono transgress the boundaries between sound, drawing, poetry, participation, movement, new media, and sculpture. They continually invoked touch as mode of connection, and they both incorporated everyday objects as charged collaborators. | Julia Bryan-Wilson

item.title: New York City’s Last Standing Wood Column Company Closes After 110 Years - Colossal
item.description:
110 years ago, Thomas Lupo’s grandfather opened the American Wood Column Corporation in Brooklyn’s Williamsburg neighborhood. Specializing in architectural woodwork including decorative moulding, columns, balusters, corbels, and more, the historic family-owned company is shutting down after more than a century. A new documentary directed and produced by filmmaker and photographer Joshua Charrow takes viewers on one final walk-through of the factory.

A vast collection of about 6,000 handmade wooden molds—many of them reverse carved molds—cover the walls and correspond to numbered samples for reference. “My grandfather bought these molds used, and they were used,” Lupo explains. “So they’ve got to be over 200 years old.”

Throughout the film, Charrow follows Lupo around the building, documenting the owner’s favorite pieces and timeless anecdotes. Among these works are six-foot pencils, ornamental department store columns, set designs from Saturday Night Live, grave details from The Godfather, The Exorcist stairway, and more.

Filled with family stories and nostalgic memories of growing up inside a woodworking studio, Lupo is cognizant of the fact that he, too, is growing older. His team, who has been with him for close to 40 years, believe it’s also time to retire gracefully. “I will be closing down the business. It’s not a question of if, it’s a question of when. That’s all.” he says. “Like anything else, everything changes. Time goes on.”

item.title: A Short Film Sheds Light on the Garfield Phones Washing Up on a French Beach Since the ’80s - Colossal
item.description:
Amid the rugged, wave-churned shoreline of France’s Breton coast, a surprising tidbit of pop culture has kept beachcombers returning for more than 40 years. The short film “Silly Little Plastic Cat” transports us to this slice of Brittany, where local residents grew up collecting parts of a 1984 Garfield-themed plastic telephone on the beach—and still do. Photographer and director Zack Grant, founder the production studio 2020 Land, was intrigued by the story, which made news a few years back after the source of the dispersed merchandise was finally discovered.

The part of Brittany where the phones wash up is situated along a busy shipping thoroughfare. At some point during their transit in the mid-1980s, the shipping container carrying thousands of the units fell into the sea, and over the years, its spilled contents have continued to arrive in distinctively orange, tangled jumbles. As quirky as it is, the phenomenon also shines a light on the less humorous side: the vast quantity of garbage that washes ashore.

To put the scale of pollution into perspective, nearly 1,500 shipping containers were lost in 2025 alone. Less than 10 percent of those were recovered; the rest are still missing. It’s a small fraction of the hundreds of millions of containers transported annually, yet a single 40-foot container could hold the contents of an entire three- or four-bedroom house or around 400 mattresses. Multiply that by several hundred and consider everything we ship—clothing, medical supplies, car parts, you name it—and we can start to scratch the surface of the oceans’ staggering garbage patches.

“Silly Little Plastic Cat” illuminates the reality of pollution and also highlights how locals are motivated to help. Residents have adopted Garfield as something of a de facto mascot for cleanup projects. “We are 100 percent responsible for the current climate situation and current pollution,” says a local conservationist who aids in beach cleanups via Surfrider Foundation. “We are also actors in the solutions.” Another initiative invites people to work together to regenerate older or damaged items, making them usable once again while reducing consumption.

See more on Grant’s work on Vimeo.

item.title: Monumental Painted Wood Carvings by Jiang Miao Center Mindfulness - Colossal
item.description:
The spiral is one of the most ubiquitous, universal symbols. Or perhaps it is more apt to describe the motif as mimicked from nature, where it occurs in the form of seashells, flowers, and curling waves. From Neolithic stone carvings at Newgrange in Ireland to swirling motifs on prehistoric pottery discovered in Thailand, the spiral represents growth, the cycles of life, and evolution. Sometimes two or more interlink, and other times they emerge from an endless line.

For artist Jiang Miao, Eastern philosophy is a touchstone. “The spiral symbolizes life, time, and the cyclical order of the universe, while color becomes a vessel for invisible energy beyond the material world,” says Whitestone Gallery, which presents the artist’s solo exhibition, Spiral of Energy.

Several series are represented in the show, including Heavenly Eyes, Mindfulness, Origin, and Taoist Trinity and the Self. “Heavenly Eyes proposes a perspective beyond ordinary human vision, contemplating the essence of existence and the order of the universe, while Mindfulness explores the nature of life through introspection and awakened consciousness,” the gallery says. Taoist Trinity and the Self is all tondos and emphasizes perpetualness. They can also be monumental: one reaches about seven feet in diameter.

Miao meticulously carves intricate textures into wood panels, then applies vibrant acrylic paint to create a sensorial movement, contrast, and glow. Both the approach and result are inherently concerned with time and concentration, spirituality and mindfulness.

Spiral of Energy continues through August 23 in Seoul. See more on the artist’s Instagram.
